data-product-framing.text: The revenue dashboard reads flat for a week and the exec team makes a hiring call on it — then someone notices the source feed stopped updating nine days ago and the warehouse just kept serving the last good partition as if it were fresh. Nobody framed the pipeline as a product with a freshness promise, so nothing ever said "this is stale."

This is lesson one of Data Engineering And Analytics Platforms, and it sets the invariant every later skill (ingestion, dbt models, reconciliation, lineage) inherits: a data product is a promise about schema, freshness, and correctness — not just code that lands rows. Frame it as a product now and every downstream lesson has a contract to enforce.

data-product-framing.prompt: "The nightly job ran green — 0 errors, exit code 0." Your revenue metric is still wrong this morning. How is that possible? Answer before reading on.
data-product-framing.reveal: Because a job succeeding and a data product being CORRECT are different axes. The job moved rows exactly as coded — it just moved stale rows (source stopped emitting), or malformed rows (a column silently became null), or duplicated rows (a partition re-ran). Exit code 0 proves the SCRIPT worked; it says nothing about whether the DATA kept its promise. That gap — green pipeline, wrong metric — is the whole reason a data product needs a contract, freshness check, and reconciliation, not just a scheduler.

data-product-framing.title: A data product is a contract: schema + freshness + a metric it must not corrupt
data-product-framing.text: Frame the pipeline as a promise, not a script. Name the source contract (expected schema), the freshness SLA (how new the data must be), the downstream metric at stake, and the feared failure. The invariant: every promise must be checkable, so a violation is caught before the warehouse — not by the CFO.

data-product-framing.title: The data product framed as a contract on the pipeline
data-product-framing.subtitle: Source → contract gate → warehouse → metric. The quality gate enforces schema + freshness BEFORE the write; on a breach, bad records are quarantined and the metric is protected. The failure path (stale/malformed data reaching the metric) is exactly what the frame exists to make visible.

data-product-framing.title: Writing the Frame — the data product contract, one line at a time
data-product-framing.subtitle: Section 1 of data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md. Each line is a promise the pipeline can be held to.
data-product-framing.code:
# Data Contract, Quality & Lineage Packet

## 1. Frame (the data product as a contract)
- Source: orders_events (Kafka topic, upstream = Orders Service)
- Schema contract: order_id:str, amount_cents:int>0, created_at:timestamp(utc), status:enum
- Freshness SLA: newest event <= 15 min behind wall clock (else STALE)
- Downstream metric at stake: daily_gross_revenue (finance dashboard)
- Feared failure: amount_cents arrives null OR feed stalls -> revenue reads low, silently
- Quality gate (before warehouse): schema check + freshness check + amount not-null
- On breach: quarantine bad partition, hold the metric at last-good, alert

<!-- Sections 2-4 (quality report, lineage map, reconciliation) added in later lessons. -->

steps.label: It is a packet, not a note
steps.note: The artifact is a reviewable data-product contract — the thing the source curriculum demands be attached to the evidence ledger and reused in the capstone.

steps.label: Name the source explicitly
steps.note: orders_events, and its upstream owner (Orders Service). A data product without a named source has no one to hold to the contract.

steps.label: The schema contract
steps.note: Types AND constraints (amount_cents:int>0). This is what a schema check enforces — a column silently going null is a contract breach, not a shrug.

steps.label: The freshness SLA
steps.note: The single most-missed clause. "<= 15 min behind" turns "is the data stale?" from a vibe into a check. No freshness SLA = the flat-dashboard failure in the mission.

steps.label: The downstream metric at stake
steps.note: daily_gross_revenue. Naming the metric is what makes the pipeline a PRODUCT — it exists to keep one number honest, not to move rows.

steps.label: The feared failure — specific
steps.note: null amount OR a stalled feed, both surfacing as revenue reading LOW. Specific enough to recognize on a dashboard, per the source's diagnose step.

steps.label: The gate + the breach behavior
steps.note: Schema + freshness + not-null BEFORE the warehouse; on breach, quarantine and hold at last-good. This is the promise made enforceable.

data-product-framing.caption: A reviewer reads these lines and knows exactly what orders_events promises and what daily_gross_revenue loses if it lies. That is a framed data product.

data-product-framing.title: Two ways to frame the same pipeline
data-product-framing.subtitle: Both load orders_events into the warehouse nightly. Only one is a data product.

left.label: A script that moves rows
lines: "ETL job: read orders topic, write to warehouse"
No schema contract — whatever arrives, lands
No freshness SLA — stale feed still exits 0
No named metric — nobody knows what breaks
Failure surfaces as a wrong number, days later
left.verdict: Green pipeline, silently corrupted metric

right.label: A framed data product
lines: Source contract: typed schema + amount_cents>0
Freshness SLA: <= 15 min or flagged STALE
Metric at stake named: daily_gross_revenue
Feared failure specific: null amount / stalled feed
Quality gate quarantines bad data before warehouse
right.verdict: A breach is caught before the metric moves

data-product-framing.caption: The difference is not more code — it is a checkable promise. "Load the table" can't be violated; "data <= 15 min fresh, amount never null" can be, and therefore can be caught.

data-product-framing.text: The senior tell, and the ACM/IEEE CS2023 data-management thread behind this course: a junior optimizes the job (make it faster, greener); a senior optimizes the CONTRACT (make a violation impossible to miss). If your pipeline can fail silently — stale, null, duplicated — and the first to notice is a human reading the metric, you built a script. A data product tells YOU it broke before it tells the CFO.

data-product-framing.question: A reviewer says: "Prove this is a framed data product, not just a load job." Which artifact detail actually proves it?
options: The pipeline ran green with exit code 0 last night.
A named source contract with a freshness SLA and a named downstream metric, plus a quality gate that quarantines a schema/freshness breach before the warehouse.
The job is scheduled nightly in the orchestrator.
The warehouse table has the right column names.
data-product-framing.explanation: Only option 2 shows a checkable PROMISE — a schema + freshness contract, the metric it protects, and a gate that catches a violation before it corrupts anything. Green runs (1), a schedule (3), and correct column names (4) all describe a script that can still serve stale or malformed data with exit code 0. The reviewer wants the contract and the breach behavior, because that is what separates a data product from a job that happens to move rows.

data-product-framing.intro: Prove your Frame is a real data-product contract — no vibes:
items: Read your source contract: does it state types AND constraints (e.g. amount_cents > 0), so a column going null is a detectable breach rather than accepted silently?
Confirm a freshness SLA exists with a concrete number ("<= 15 min"). If "stale" is a feeling, not a threshold, the flat-dashboard failure can still happen.
Check exactly one downstream metric is named. If the pipeline protects no named number, it is a load job, not a product.
Confirm the feared failure is specific enough to recognize on a dashboard or in a reconciliation report — "data is bad" is not specific; "revenue reads low because amount arrived null" is.
Verify the quality gate runs BEFORE the warehouse write and says what happens on breach (quarantine + hold at last-good), so bad data cannot reach the metric while you are asleep.

prompts: In your own words: why does a pipeline exiting with code 0 tell you nothing about whether the data product kept its promise?
Explain the difference between a schema check and a freshness check using your own contract — what does each one catch that the other misses?
Which single downstream metric does your data product protect, and what is the exact feared failure that would corrupt it silently if you had no contract?

data-product-framing.text: The move is domain-independent: any feed a decision depends on becomes a product the moment you write down its contract. Point the same frame at a new source (a third-party API instead of Kafka), a schema-drift case (upstream renames a column), or a late-arriving-data case (events land hours after their event time) — the invariant stays (schema + freshness + a named metric, all checkable), only the specific promise and gate change. This packet — data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md — is the same artifact the capstone reuses: next lessons grow it with the quality report, the lineage map, and the metric reconciliation, turning "I framed one data product" into a full pipeline you can hand a reviewer.

A reviewer runs the contract check against a deliberately broken feed and sees it FAIL loudly, not silently pass.

source-contracts.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have a source contract if it only validates the happy path. A contract that cannot fail on a stale partition, a nulled key, or a type-drifted column is documentation, not a contract. The proof is a rejection, not a green run.

source-contracts.text: The revenue dashboard reads clean at 9am and the CFO screenshots it — but the upstream vendor silently shipped yesterday's file twice and dropped a currency column, so "revenue" is quietly 18% wrong and nobody knows until finance reconciles a week later. No source contract meant no gate, and the bad data walked straight into the metric.

A source contract is the enforced agreement between a pipeline and every feed it ingests: schema, freshness, and quality constraints that MUST hold before data is trusted. It is Section 1 of the data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md you carry through this course — the gate that stops corrupt source data before it becomes a corrupt warehouse table.

source-contracts.prompt: Your nightly load succeeded — zero errors, all rows written to the warehouse. Is your data correct? Decide before reading on.
source-contracts.reveal: A successful load proves the bytes moved, not that they mean anything. "No errors" catches broken syntax; it is blind to a stale partition (yesterday's file re-delivered), a silently nulled join key, or a type that drifted from cents to dollars. Those corrupt the metric while every job stays green. The contract is what turns "it ran" into "it is trustworthy" — it asserts what the data must BE, not just that it arrived.

source-contracts.title: A source contract asserts schema + freshness + quality — and can reject
source-contracts.text: Pin the required schema (columns, types, nullability), a freshness SLA (max lag from event to partition), and value constraints (ranges, keys, enums). The invariant: bad data is quarantined at ingestion, never served. A contract that cannot reject is decoration.

source-contracts.title: The source contract as an ingestion gate
source-contracts.subtitle: Vendor feed → contract gate → warehouse → metric. The gate splits the flow: conforming partitions land; violations quarantine and page. The failure path (stale/malformed) and the repair path (backfill after fix) are both marked.

legend.label: the gate that enforces the contract
failure path — quarantine, do not serve

source-contracts.title: Writing the contract, one assertion at a time
source-contracts.subtitle: A dbt source with tests + a freshness SLA — the enforceable core of data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md.
source-contracts.code:
sources:
  - name: vendor_orders
    loaded_at_field: ingested_at
    freshness:
      warn_after: { count: 6, period: hour }
      error_after: { count: 24, period: hour }   # freshness SLA
    tables:
      - name: orders_daily
        columns:
          - name: order_id
            tests: [unique, not_null]              # key constraint
          - name: amount_cents
            tests:
              - not_null
              - dbt_utils.accepted_range:
                  min_value: 0                     # no negative revenue
          - name: currency
            tests:
              - not_null
              - accepted_values: { values: ['USD','EUR','GBP'] }
        # quarantine: on failure, dbt build stops the metric model downstream

steps.label: Name the source, pin the freshness field
steps.note: loaded_at_field is what freshness is measured against. Without it, a re-delivered stale partition looks identical to a fresh one — the exact failure from the mission.

steps.label: The freshness SLA
steps.note: error_after: 24h means a partition older than a day fails the build. This is the freshness half of the contract — lag is a first-class violation, not a warning you ignore.

steps.label: Key integrity
steps.note: unique + not_null on order_id. A nulled or duplicated key is the silent corruption that double-counts revenue. The contract makes it a hard stop.

steps.label: Range constraint
steps.note: amount_cents >= 0. Negative revenue is physically impossible; a type drift (dollars written as cents, or a sign flip) trips this before it reaches the metric.

steps.label: Enum on currency
steps.note: The dropped/garbled currency column from the mission fails accepted_values. A NULL or 'XXX' currency is caught at the source, not discovered in reconciliation.

steps.label: Quarantine by construction
steps.note: In dbt, a failing source test halts the downstream metric model. Bad data cannot be served — it is quarantined and the run pages. That IS the contract's teeth.

source-contracts.caption: Run it against a stale, currency-dropped partition: freshness errors AND accepted_values fails — the metric model never builds. Rejection is the proof.

source-contracts.title: A load job vs a real source contract
source-contracts.subtitle: Same feed: "vendor_orders arrives nightly." Both feel like a pipeline. Only one protects the metric.

left.label: Load and hope
lines: COPY the file into the warehouse, log 'success'
No freshness check — a re-sent file loads clean
No key test — nulled order_id silently double-counts
No range/enum — dropped currency becomes NULL revenue
Failure is discovered downstream, in reconciliation, days late

Stale partition → freshness error, build halts
Bad records quarantined with a report, on-call paged
Lineage records which source + partition fed the metric
Backfill path re-ingests only after the vendor fixes the feed

source-contracts.caption: The difference is not more code — it is a gate that can say NO. A pipeline that can only succeed is not enforcing a contract, it is transporting whatever it is handed.

source-contracts.text: The senior tell on data quality: enforce constraints at the boundary you do not control, not the one you do. Junior teams validate their own transforms and trust the vendor; the failure almost always enters at the source you cannot see. The contract lives on the untrusted edge — that is where it earns its keep.

source-contracts.question: A reviewer asks you to prove your source contract is real, not happy-path theater. Which piece of evidence actually proves it?
options: A screenshot of the nightly load succeeding with zero errors.
A run against a deliberately stale, currency-dropped partition that FAILS the freshness + accepted_values checks and quarantines the records, with the bad-record report attached.
A written description of the schema you expect from the vendor.
A dashboard showing revenue looked correct last week.
source-contracts.explanation: Only option 2 shows the contract exercising its one job — rejecting bad data. A successful load (1) proves transport, not correctness; a schema description (3) is documentation with no teeth; a good-looking dashboard (4) is exactly the silent-failure trap the contract exists to break. The proof of a contract is a rejection you can point to.

source-contracts.intro: Prove your source contract holds — no vibes:
items: Point to a run where a malformed or stale partition FAILED the contract and was quarantined. If every run you can show is green, you have not proven it can reject.
Confirm the freshness SLA has a concrete threshold measured against a real loaded_at field — not 'we assume it is daily'.
Check every business key has unique + not_null; a nulled or duplicated key is the classic silent double-count.
Confirm at least one value constraint (range or enum) that would catch a type drift or a dropped column — the mission's failure.
Show the bad-record quarantine report and the lineage entry naming which source + partition fed the metric, so a reviewer can trace corruption to its origin.

prompts: In your own words: why does a successful load say nothing about whether the data is correct, and what does the contract add on top?
Explain freshness as a first-class contract term using your own feed: what stale partition would slip through with no SLA, and what breaks downstream?
Walk the failure path and the repair path on your own diagram: a partition violates the contract — what happens to it, who is paged, and how does clean data eventually get in?

source-contracts.text: The same contract pattern travels to every new source and every drift case. A late-arriving streaming feed gets a watermark-based freshness SLA instead of a daily one; a schema-drift case (vendor renames a column) gets a schema-registry check that fails the build the moment the shape changes; a governance constraint (PII must never land unmasked) becomes a not_null-style assertion on the masked column. What stays invariant: the gate can reject, bad records quarantine, lineage records origin. What changes: the freshness unit, the constraint set, and the blast radius as scale, latency, and privacy risk rise. Next you take this exact data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md into ingestion and orchestration — the contract you wrote here is the gate every DAG downstream depends on, and the first reusable piece of your data-platform capstone evidence.

ingestion-patterns.proof: Section 'Ingestion' of data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md: the named source, the chosen pattern with its selected/rejected justification, the partition/watermark key, the schema contract, a freshness SLO, and a quarantine rule for malformed rows. A reviewer can trace one bad record from source to its quarantine without you narrating.
ingestion-patterns.unlock: Your packet names the pattern, defends why the rejected pattern was wrong for THIS feed, and shows the schema + freshness + quarantine guards that catch stale or malformed data before it reaches a metric.
ingestion-patterns.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have an ingestion pattern if the load simply overwrites the table every run with no watermark, no freshness check, and no quarantine. A pipe that trusts the source blindly is not a pattern — it is a way to corrupt a metric quietly on the first bad file.

ingestion-patterns.text: Monday's revenue dashboard reads 40% low. Nobody deployed. The cause: Friday's vendor changed a column type, the loader coerced every price to NULL, and the pipeline ingested it without a word — because the ingestion pattern trusted the source instead of contracting with it.

Ingestion is the seam where the outside world enters your warehouse, and every downstream metric, dbt model, and lineage graph inherits whatever it lets through. Choosing the pattern — and the guards around it — is the first place a data product earns or loses trust.

ingestion-patterns.prompt: A vendor sends you a daily file of all orders. Easiest load: TRUNCATE the table, load the file, done. What breaks the first week — and what were you actually trusting?
ingestion-patterns.reveal: You trusted that every file is complete and well-formed — and neither is guaranteed. The day the vendor ships a partial file, your full-refresh silently deletes yesterday's rows too; the day a column type drifts, you overwrite good history with NULLs. Full-snapshot isn't wrong, but WITHOUT a row-count floor, a schema contract, and a freshness check it is a single bad file away from erasing the truth. The pattern is never just 'how you load' — it's 'what you refuse to load.'

ingestion-patterns.title: An ingestion pattern is a contract, not a pipe
ingestion-patterns.text: Pick the load shape the source's change behavior demands — full-snapshot, incremental append, CDC, or streaming — then bind it to a schema contract, a freshness SLO, and a quarantine for bad rows. The invariant: no unverified source data reaches a metric.

ingestion-patterns.title: The ingestion path — with its failure branch and its repair branch
ingestion-patterns.subtitle: A source lands in raw, passes three gates (schema · freshness · row-quality), then loads to the warehouse and feeds a metric. Fail any gate and the batch is quarantined and alerted — never merged. Repair re-runs the same gates.

legend.label: the gates — where the pattern becomes a contract
failure path — bad batch quarantined, never merged
only validated data reaches the metric

ingestion-patterns.title: Writing the Ingestion section — an incremental load with guards
ingestion-patterns.subtitle: The real artifact: a watermarked incremental append with schema, freshness, and quarantine checks. This is what makes the pattern safe.
ingestion-patterns.code:
# Ingestion: orders_daily  (pattern: incremental append, watermark = updated_at)
EXPECTED_SCHEMA = {"order_id": "str", "amount": "float", "updated_at": "timestamp"}
FRESHNESS_SLO_HOURS = 6          # newest row must be < 6h old
ROW_FLOOR = 500                 # a full day is never < 500 orders

def ingest(batch, last_watermark):
    assert_schema(batch, EXPECTED_SCHEMA)                 # schema contract
    new_rows = [r for r in batch if r.updated_at > last_watermark]
    if hours_since(max(r.updated_at for r in new_rows)) > FRESHNESS_SLO_HOURS:
        raise Quarantine("stale source: newest row exceeds freshness SLO")
    if len(new_rows) < ROW_FLOOR:
        raise Quarantine(f"row floor breached: {len(new_rows)} < {ROW_FLOOR}")
    good, bad = partition_valid(new_rows)                 # amount not null, order_id unique
    quarantine(bad)                                       # bad rows held, not dropped
    load_append(good, partition="load_date")
    return max(r.updated_at for r in good)                # advance watermark

steps.label: Name the pattern + its schema contract
steps.note: Incremental append with an updated_at watermark — chosen because orders are updated in place, not just inserted. EXPECTED_SCHEMA is the contract the source must honor.

steps.label: Freshness SLO and row floor as constants
steps.note: Two numbers that encode 'what normal looks like.' A day of orders is never under 500 and never older than 6 hours — deviations are signals, not data.

steps.label: Schema check first — fail fast
steps.note: assert_schema runs before any logic. A drifted column type (the Monday-40%-low bug) dies here instead of coercing prices to NULL downstream.

steps.label: The watermark — the heart of incremental
steps.note: Only rows newer than last_watermark are new work. This is what makes it incremental, not full-refresh: no re-scanning, no accidental history deletion.

steps.label: Freshness + row-floor quarantine
steps.note: A stale feed or a partial file raises Quarantine BEFORE loading. The batch is held and alerted — the pipeline refuses to poison the metric.

steps.label: Row-quality split: good loads, bad is HELD not dropped
steps.note: Malformed rows go to quarantine, not the floor. Quarantine is inspectable evidence for reconciliation; dropping is silent data loss.

steps.label: Advance the watermark only on success
steps.note: The watermark moves only after a clean load. A quarantined batch leaves it untouched, so the repaired re-run picks up exactly where it stopped — idempotent by construction.

ingestion-patterns.caption: Every guard here is a line in the lineage story: source → schema → freshness → row-quality → warehouse. Trace a bad row and it stops at quarantine, never at the metric.

ingestion-patterns.caption: The difference isn't the load mechanism — it's what each one refuses to load. The contracted pattern turns 'silent corruption' into 'a loud, inspectable quarantine.'

ingestion-patterns.text: The senior tell in ingestion is the row floor and the freshness SLO, not the loader. Anyone can wire a pipe; a data engineer encodes what 'normal' looks like as a number the pipeline can enforce — so a partial file or a stalled vendor trips an alert at 3 a.m. instead of surfacing as a wrong number in the Monday board review. DORA's research associates strong delivery performance with fast recovery, but it does not prescribe a specific automated failure-signal technique.

ingestion-patterns.question: A reviewer says: 'Show me the exact evidence that this ingestion is not just a happy-path answer.' Which response actually proves it?
options: "It uses an incremental append pattern with a watermark, which is the modern best practice."
"Here is the quarantine report from the partial-file run: 312 rows held, the row-floor alert that fired, and the watermark that stayed put so the repaired re-run resumed cleanly."
"The pipeline has run green every day this week, so it works."
"We load into a partitioned staging table and dbt models read from it downstream."
ingestion-patterns.explanation: Only option 2 points at the failure path made concrete: a real quarantine report, the alert that fired, and the watermark behavior that made the re-run safe. Naming the pattern (1), a green streak (3), or the downstream wiring (4) all describe the happy path — the reviewer asked for the evidence that the BAD case is handled, which is exactly what quarantine + freshness + row-floor produce.

ingestion-patterns.intro: Prove your ingestion pattern is a contract, not a pipe:
items: Schema check: point to the exact line that fails the batch on a column type drift. If a bad type would coerce to NULL and load, you have no contract.
Freshness: name the SLO in hours and show the check that quarantines a stale batch before it loads — not a dashboard you'd notice later.
Row-quality: confirm malformed rows are QUARANTINED (held + inspectable), not dropped. Dropped rows are silent data loss with no lineage.
Watermark/idempotency: confirm a quarantined batch leaves the watermark untouched, so a repaired re-run resumes exactly where it stopped and never double-loads.
Reconciliation: you can produce a bad-record quarantine report and a row count that ties the loaded partition back to the source count.

prompts: In your own words: why is 'TRUNCATE and reload the whole file' a way to lose history, and what one guard prevents it?
Explain the difference between quarantining a malformed row and dropping it — using lineage and reconciliation to make the case.
Which pattern did you choose for your feed (full-snapshot, incremental, CDC, streaming), and what did the source's change behavior force that choice — not your preference?

ingestion-patterns.text: The pattern travels to every new source. A late-arriving-data feed keeps the same contract but swaps the watermark for an event-time window with a grace period. A schema-drift-prone vendor keeps the same schema check but adds a versioned contract and an owner alert. A streaming source keeps freshness + quarantine but trades the batch row-floor for a rolling-rate SLO. What stays invariant: no unverified source data reaches a metric, and every rejected batch is held and named. What changes is the watermark and the SLO, driven by the source's latency, volume, and risk. Carry data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md into the capstone — its schema check, freshness SLO, quarantine report, and lineage map are exactly the evidence the data-platform capstone reuses to prove the pipeline is trustworthy, not just wired.

The cause is not the metric query — it is a source file that arrived empty six hours ago, and the pipeline loaded it anyway because nothing stood between the stale extract and the warehouse.

An orchestration DAG is the backbone of every data product: it turns a pile of extract, load, and transform steps into an ordered, observable graph where each task's success is the precondition for the next. orchestration-dags.title: Wiring the DAG so the gate cannot be skipped
orchestration-dags.subtitle: An Airflow DAG where load DEPENDS on a passing freshness+schema check. Order is expressed as dependency edges, not as line order.
orchestration-dags.code:
from airflow import DAG
from airflow.operators.python import PythonOperator
from airflow.exceptions import AirflowFailException
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

def validate_source(**ctx):
    part = extract_partition(ctx["ds"])          # today's raw partition
    age = now() - part.max_event_ts
    if age > timedelta(hours=2):                  # FRESHNESS contract
        raise AirflowFailException(f"stale: {age} old")
    missing = REQUIRED_COLS - set(part.columns)   # SCHEMA contract
    if missing or len(part) == 0:                 # empty == malformed
        raise AirflowFailException(f"bad schema/empty: {missing}")

with DAG("orders_metric", schedule="@daily",
         default_args={"retries": 2, "retry_delay": timedelta(minutes=5)},
         catchup=False, start_date=datetime(2026, 1, 1)) as dag:
    extract   = PythonOperator(task_id="extract_source",  python_callable=pull_source)
    validate  = PythonOperator(task_id="validate_source", python_callable=validate_source)
    load      = PythonOperator(task_id="load_warehouse",  python_callable=upsert_staging)
    transform = PythonOperator(task_id="dbt_transform",   python_callable=run_dbt_model)
    reconcile = PythonOperator(task_id="reconcile_metric",python_callable=check_totals)

    extract >> validate >> load >> transform >> reconcile   # edges = the contract

steps.label: The freshness contract
steps.note: The gate fails the TASK if the newest event is older than the SLA. Because a raised exception fails validate_source, its downstream (load) is skipped — the stale partition never reaches the warehouse.

steps.label: The schema + empty contract
steps.note: Missing required columns or zero rows is malformed by definition. An empty file is the most common silent killer — treat it as a hard failure, not a quiet no-op.

steps.label: Retries make transient failures self-heal
steps.note: retries=2 with a 5-min delay lets a flaky source recover without paging anyone — but a genuinely stale partition still fails all attempts and halts. Retry is not a substitute for the gate.

steps.label: catchup=False
steps.note: Without this, a paused DAG floods backfill runs on resume. Foundation gotcha: idempotent tasks + explicit catchup keep backfills safe.

steps.label: Dependencies ARE the order
steps.note: extract >> validate >> load is the whole point: the graph — not the file's line order — guarantees load only runs after validate passes. Reorder the file and behavior is identical; cut one edge and the gate is bypassed.

orchestration-dags.text: The pattern is invariant; the contract changes with the source. Apply it to a NEW source with schema drift — a vendor renames a column mid-quarter — and the schema gate fails the run instead of loading nulls into the metric; you widen validate_source, not the whole DAG. Apply it to LATE-ARRIVING data — the gate's freshness window and a sensor/wait-for-partition task change, but extract >> validate >> load and reconcile stay put. What always holds: the load is gated, failures halt-and-quarantine, and reconciliation blocks publish. What changes by source, scale, and SLA: the freshness threshold, the retry budget, and the partition strategy. This same data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md — DAG, gate, quarantine report, reconciliation — is the artifact your data-platform capstone reuses; the portfolio claim names the proof ('caught a stale partition at the gate before it hit the revenue metric'), not just the topic.

Bronze is the first landing zone of a data platform: source data captured exactly as it arrived, before any cleaning, so every downstream silver model, metric, and reconciliation has a replayable ground truth. raw-bronze-layer.text: Treat data provenance as a first-class quality attribute — and the senior tell is quarantine over silence. raw-bronze-layer.explanation: Bronze is defined by replayable provenance, not volume, tidiness, or a green light. Option 2 is the only one that proves fidelity (reproduce the source), lineage (the three stamps), and honest handling of bad data (quarantine + count). Clean, renamed columns (3) are actually evidence AGAINST bronze — that is silver's job. A green pipeline (4) can hide silently dropped rows.

raw-bronze-layer.intro: Prove your Bronze Layer holds — no vibes:
items: Schema check: run the contract against a good file (PASSES) and a malformed file (FAILS and routes rows to quarantine). If the malformed file passes, your contract is decoration.
Freshness check: query max(_loaded_at) per source. If it is older than the feed's SLA, the load is stale — the check should flag it, not you noticing later.
Lineage: pick any row and trace it back to its _source_file. If you cannot name the exact file a row came from, you have data without provenance.
Append-only: re-run the load on the same partition. Row count must not shrink and existing rows must not change. If they do, you have an UPSERT, not bronze.
Quarantine + reconciliation: rows landed + rows quarantined must equal rows in the source file. A gap means rows were silently dropped — the failure this lesson exists to kill.

A new API feed, a schema that gains a column overnight, a late-arriving correction that lands three days after the fact — the move is identical: land it untouched, stamp its lineage, partition by ingest date, quarantine what fails, transform nothing. Staging is one source, cleaned — the moment it fans out or rolls up, the lineage stops being trustworthy and the contract stops meaning anything.

staging-models.text: A revenue dashboard reads 12% low all quarter, and three analysts each patched a different downstream model to "fix" it. The real cause: the raw Stripe export renamed amount to amount_cents mid-month, and no staging model stood between the raw file and the metric to catch it.

A staging model is the one clean, contracted doorway between a raw source and everything you build on it — rename, cast, and lightly validate once, so every downstream model inherits a stable, tested column. Without it, schema drift and stale partitions leak straight into your metrics.

staging-models.prompt: You need customer email lowercased and a cents-to-dollars cast for a revenue mart. Where does that transformation belong — in the staging model, or the mart? Answer before reading on.
staging-models.reveal: Split it. Lowercasing email and casting amount_cents to a numeric are one-to-one cleanup of the SOURCE — they belong in staging, done once, so every mart inherits them. Dividing by 100 to express dollars, or joining customers to charges, is BUSINESS logic — it belongs in the mart. The tell: staging changes the shape of a column; a mart changes the meaning of a row. Put business logic in staging and you have quietly forked the source contract for every consumer downstream.

-- models/staging/stripe/stg_stripe__charges.sql
with source as (
    select * from {{ source('stripe', 'charges') }}
),
renamed as (
    select
        id                       as charge_id,
        customer                 as customer_id,
        cast(amount_cents as bigint) as amount_cents,
        lower(receipt_email)     as receipt_email,
        status                   as charge_status,
        cast(created as timestamp) as created_at
    from source
)
select * from renamed

-- models/staging/stripe/_stripe__sources.yml
sources:
  - name: stripe
    freshness:
      warn_after:  {count: 6,  period: hour}
      error_after: {count: 24, period: hour}
    loaded_at_field: created
    tables:
      - name: charges
        columns:
          - name: id
            tests: [unique, not_null]
          - name: amount_cents
            tests: [not_null]

steps.note: {{ source('stripe','charges') }} — never a hard-coded raw table name. This is the lineage edge dbt tracks and the freshness contract binds to. A ref to the raw table by name breaks both.

steps.label: Rename to house convention
steps.note: id -> charge_id, customer -> customer_id. Every downstream model now speaks one vocabulary. This is the one-to-one cleanup staging exists for.

steps.label: Light normalization only
steps.note: lower(receipt_email) is column-shape cleanup — fine. Dividing amount_cents by 100 to make dollars would be business logic — that belongs in the mart, not here.

transformations-marts.outcome: Take one raw source table and build a two-layer dbt transformation into a mart — a staging model that cleans + tests the source, and a mart model that computes ONE business metric — then gate the mart on a freshness + data-quality check so stale or malformed source data can never silently corrupt the metric.
transformations-marts.proof: data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md plus the two dbt models (stg_*.sql, mart_*.sql) and their schema.yml tests. The packet names: the source contract, the metric the mart owns, the freshness threshold, the quarantine rule for bad records, and a metric-reconciliation number (mart total vs source total). A reviewer runs `dbt build` and sees the freshness/quality test FAIL on stale input and PASS on clean input.
transformations-marts.unlock: Your mart is downstream of a tested staging model, the metric reconciles to source within tolerance, and a freshness test blocks the build when the partition is stale.
transformations-marts.doNotClaim: Do not claim the mart is 'trustworthy' if the only test is that the SQL runs. A model that compiles on malformed data is not verified — it is a metric that will lie confidently. The proof is a test that FAILS on bad source data, not one that always passes.

transformations-marts.text: Monday 8 a.m.: the revenue dashboard reads $0 for a top region. The mart SQL ran green, dbt reported success — but an upstream job stopped landing the orders partition Friday night, and the mart happily aggregated an empty table into a confident, wrong number that a VP already screenshotted.

A mart is a metric other people trust without reading the SQL — so its job is not just to transform, but to refuse to serve a number it cannot stand behind. This lesson turns raw source rows into a governed metric with staging, tests, freshness, and lineage: Section by section, the reviewable packet you carry into the capstone.

transformations-marts.prompt: Your mart model `SELECT sum(amount) FROM orders` ran successfully and returned a number. Is a successful run enough to trust that number? Decide before reading.
transformations-marts.reveal: No — a run proves the SQL is valid, not that the DATA is. `sum(amount)` over a partition that never loaded returns 0, not an error. Over a partition with duplicated rows it returns double. The query succeeds in every case; correctness lives one layer up, in the source contract: is the partition fresh, are the rows unique, is `amount` non-null? A mart without a freshness + quality gate doesn't fail loudly — it fails as a plausible wrong number, which is the most expensive failure in analytics.

transformations-marts.title: A mart is a metric with a contract, not just a SELECT
transformations-marts.text: Stage the source (clean + test it), then compute the metric in the mart. The invariant: the mart may only serve a number whose source is FRESH and PASSES data-quality tests. Freshness + tests gate the metric; lineage records where it came from.

transformations-marts.title: The staging → mart pipeline, with the failure and repair paths
transformations-marts.subtitle: Raw orders flow through a tested staging model into the revenue mart. When the source partition is stale or malformed, the freshness/quality gate diverts bad records to quarantine and FAILS the build (red path) instead of serving a corrupted metric. The repair path re-runs after backfill.

legend.label: failure path — stale/bad data quarantined, build fails

transformations-marts.title: The mart, its test, and the freshness gate
transformations-marts.subtitle: stg_orders cleans the source; schema.yml tests it; the source freshness block fails the build when the partition is stale.
transformations-marts.code:
-- stg_orders.sql — clean the source before anyone aggregates it
with source as (
    select * from {{ source('raw', 'orders') }}
),
cleaned as (
    select
        order_id,
        cast(order_date as date) as order_date,
        coalesce(amount, 0)      as amount,
        row_number() over (
            partition by order_id order by ingested_at desc
        ) as rn                     -- dedupe: keep latest per order_id
    from source
)
select order_id, order_date, amount
from cleaned where rn = 1 and amount >= 0

-- mart_daily_revenue.sql — the metric, built ONLY on tested staging
select order_date, sum(amount) as daily_revenue, count(*) as orders
from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
group by order_date

-- schema.yml — the contract that makes the metric refuse to lie
# sources:  raw.orders:  freshness: {warn_after: 6h, error_after: 24h}
# models:   stg_orders:  order_id  -> unique, not_null
#                        amount    -> not_null
#           mart_daily_revenue: daily_revenue -> not_null

steps.label: Reference the SOURCE, not a hardcode
steps.note: `{{ source('raw','orders') }}` is the source contract's anchor — it is what dbt freshness checks and what lineage tracks. Never `FROM raw.orders` directly.

steps.label: Dedupe the partition
steps.note: A re-landed partition duplicates rows; `row_number()` keeps the latest per order_id. Without this, SUM(amount) double-counts and the metric silently inflates.

steps.label: Drop malformed rows
steps.note: `rn = 1 and amount >= 0` is the quarantine boundary — negative or duplicate rows never reach the mart. In production the dropped rows go to a bad-record table, not the void.

steps.label: The mart builds on ref(), not the raw source
steps.note: `{{ ref('stg_orders') }}` means the mart is downstream of the TESTED model. Lineage is now: raw.orders -> stg_orders -> mart_daily_revenue, computable by dbt.

steps.label: The freshness + quality contract
steps.note: error_after: 24h fails the build if the partition is stale — the Monday-8am scenario. unique/not_null on order_id catch dupes and gaps BEFORE they reach the metric.

transformations-marts.caption: `dbt build` runs staging → tests → mart in dependency order. Stale source or a failed unique test aborts before the mart materializes — the metric is never served wrong.

transformations-marts.text: The senior move is source freshness as a build blocker, not a dashboard footnote. Juniors test the mart's output; seniors test the mart's INPUT contract — because a metric computed on stale or duplicated source is wrong no matter how clean the SQL is. DORA does not have a 'quality gates before delivery' doctrine; it measures delivery outcomes, not gate placement. Rephrase: 'Grounded in CS2023 data-management practice: the gate lives upstream of the number, not beside it.'

transformations-marts.question: A reviewer says: 'Show me the exact evidence that this mart isn't just a happy-path SELECT.' Which single artifact proves it?
options: The mart SQL compiling and returning rows in the warehouse.
A screenshot of the dashboard showing a plausible revenue number.
A dbt run where the freshness/unique test FAILS on a stale or duplicated partition and blocks the build, plus a metric-reconciliation showing mart total = source total within tolerance.
A comment in the SQL explaining that the data is trustworthy.
transformations-marts.explanation: Only option 3 is falsifiable evidence: a test that can return 'fail' and does so on bad input proves the gate works, and reconciliation proves the transform didn't drop or duplicate value. Options 1, 2, and 4 all pass on corrupted data — a compiling query, a plausible number, and a comment are exactly what a silently-wrong mart also produces.

transformations-marts.intro: Prove the mart earns trust — no vibes:
items: Run `dbt source freshness` against a deliberately stale partition — the build must ERROR, not warn-and-continue. If it serves the metric anyway, your gate is decoration.
Duplicate one order_id in the source and run the `unique` test — it must fail. Then confirm your staging dedupe makes it pass. A test that can't fail proves nothing.
Reconcile: compare `SUM(amount)` on raw.orders vs `SUM(daily_revenue)` on the mart. They must match within your stated tolerance — a gap means staging silently dropped or doubled rows.
Trace lineage: `dbt` should show raw.orders -> stg_orders -> mart_daily_revenue. If the mart selects from the raw source directly, lineage is broken and freshness never gates it.
Check the quarantine report exists: the malformed/duplicate rows dropped in staging are recorded somewhere inspectable, not discarded into a WHERE clause.

transformations-marts.title: Two marts, same source
transformations-marts.subtitle: Both compute daily revenue. Only one refuses to serve a wrong number.

left.label: Bare SELECT mart
lines: `SELECT sum(amount) FROM raw.orders`
Reads the raw source directly — no staging
No freshness check: stale partition → returns 0
No unique test: re-landed rows → double-counts
No lineage dbt can trace, no reconciliation
Run is green on empty AND on duplicated data
left.verdict: Fails as a confident wrong number

right.label: Contract-gated mart
lines: Builds on `ref('stg_orders')`, a tested model
Staging dedupes + drops malformed rows
`error_after: 24h` blocks build on stale source
`unique`/`not_null` catch dupes and gaps first
Lineage: raw -> stg -> mart, freshness gated
Reconciles: mart total = source total ± tolerance
right.verdict: Refuses to serve; fails loudly + repairable

transformations-marts.caption: A mart's value is not that it computes a number — it's that it won't hand you a number it can't stand behind.

transformations-marts.text: Same pattern, new pressure. A late-arriving-data source (events that land hours after their event_date) changes the freshness threshold and forces an incremental mart with a lookback window — but the invariant holds: stage, test, gate, reconcile, trace lineage. A schema-drift case (source adds/renames a column) is caught by the same not_null/contract tests instead of silently nulling the metric. A privacy constraint changes WHAT the mart may expose (aggregate only, no PII passthrough) but not the gate. Carry `data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md` into the data-platform capstone: it is your proof of a governed metric — schema check, freshness check, lineage map, quarantine report, and reconciliation — not just 'I wrote some dbt.'

incremental-processing.outcome: Take one real (or realistic) pipeline that reloads a whole table every run and convert it to INCREMENTAL: pick a watermark column, process only rows newer than the last successful run, and handle late-arriving data with a bounded look-back window — then package the decision as a reviewable artifact.
incremental-processing.proof: The `data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md` artifact with an Incremental Processing section: named watermark column, the incremental predicate, the late-data look-back window, a freshness check, and a metric-reconciliation number proving the incremental run matches a full refresh. A reviewer can re-run it and get the same row counts.
incremental-processing.unlock: Your pipeline reads only new/changed partitions since the last watermark, quarantines bad records instead of corrupting the metric, and reconciles to a full refresh within tolerance.
incremental-processing.doNotClaim: Do not claim a pipeline is 'incremental' just because it runs on a schedule. A cron that still `SELECT *`s the whole source every run is a full refresh with a timer. Incremental means the WORK scales with the new data, not the table size — and the watermark is durable across failures.

incremental-processing.text: The nightly job used to finish in eight minutes; now the orders table has 400M rows and it takes six hours, blows the warehouse budget, and finishes after the morning exec dashboard is already wrong. Nobody added logic — the data just grew, and the pipeline reprocesses all of history every single night.

Incremental Processing is the hinge between a toy pipeline and a production data product: it makes cost and latency scale with NEW data, not total data. It sits between your source contract and your warehouse models — get it wrong and every downstream metric, lineage edge, and freshness SLA inherits the damage.

incremental-processing.prompt: You switch a pipeline to 'only load rows where created_at > last_run_time'. It runs fast and looks correct for a week. Then a metric silently drifts low. What did the watermark miss? Answer before reading on.
incremental-processing.reveal: Late-arriving data. A row can be CREATED at 11:58pm but LAND in the source at 12:03am — after your watermark already advanced past 11:58. Filtering on `created_at > last_run` silently drops it forever. The fix is not a bigger watermark; it is a bounded LOOK-BACK window (reprocess the last N hours every run and upsert), trading a little redundant work for zero silent loss. 'Fast and correct for a week' is exactly how incremental bugs hide — they only surface as slow metric drift, never as an error.

incremental-processing.title: Incremental = watermark + look-back + idempotent upsert
incremental-processing.text: Track the last successfully processed point (the watermark). Each run reads only rows past it MINUS a look-back window to catch late data, then upserts by key so re-processing is idempotent. Invariant: the incremental result must equal a full refresh.

incremental-processing.title: The incremental load path — where lag and late data hide
incremental-processing.subtitle: Source → watermark-bounded read → quarantine → idempotent upsert into the warehouse. The late-data look-back is the loop that catches the 11:58pm-created / 12:03am-landed row; malformed rows divert to quarantine instead of poisoning the metric.

legend.label: idempotent upsert — result must equal full refresh

incremental-processing.title: An incremental dbt model, line by line
incremental-processing.subtitle: The real artifact: a dbt incremental model with a look-back window and idempotent upsert — the gold version from the worked example.
incremental-processing.code:
{{ config(
    materialized='incremental',
    unique_key='order_id',
    incremental_strategy='merge'
) }}

select
    order_id,
    customer_id,
    amount,
    created_at,
    _loaded_at
from {{ source('shop', 'orders') }}
where amount is not null

{% if is_incremental() %}
  -- look back 3h past the last load to catch late-arriving events
  and _loaded_at > (select max(_loaded_at) from {{ this }}) - interval '3 hours'
{% endif %}

steps.label: Materialize incremental, not table
steps.note: materialized='incremental' means dbt builds the full table once, then only MERGEs new rows on later runs. This is the switch that makes work scale with new data, not table size.

steps.label: unique_key = the idempotency contract
steps.note: order_id is the merge key. Re-processing the same row upserts instead of duplicating — this is what makes the look-back window safe to replay every run.

steps.label: merge strategy
steps.note: 'merge' upserts by unique_key; a naive 'append' would double-count every row inside the look-back window. Strategy choice IS the correctness decision.

steps.label: Reject before you compute
steps.note: amount is not null diverts malformed rows out of the metric path. Enforced in the source contract, this is your quarantine gate — bad records never reach revenue.

steps.label: The watermark predicate
steps.note: is_incremental() only fires on incremental runs. `_loaded_at > max(_loaded_at)` is the watermark; the pipeline reads only fresh partitions instead of the whole 400M-row history.

steps.label: The look-back window (the whole lesson)
steps.note: − interval '3 hours' deliberately re-reads the last 3h so a row created at 11:58pm but landed at 12:03am is still picked up. Idempotent merge makes the redundant re-read free of duplicates.

incremental-processing.caption: Filter on _loaded_at (when it LANDED), never created_at (when it happened) — landing time is what your watermark can actually observe.

incremental-processing.title: Watermark-only vs watermark + look-back
incremental-processing.subtitle: Same source, same schedule. Both run fast. Only one reconciles to a full refresh.

left.label: Naive watermark (silent loss)
lines: Filter: created_at > last_run_time
append strategy (no unique_key)
Late row (created 11:58, landed 12:03) dropped forever
No quarantine — a null amount nulls the metric
Passes for a week, then revenue drifts ~2% low
No reconciliation step — nobody notices
left.verdict: Fast, wrong, and invisible until a metric audit

right.label: Look-back + idempotent merge (gold)
lines: Filter: _loaded_at > max(_loaded_at) − 3h
merge on unique_key=order_id (idempotent)
Late-landing rows caught by the 3h window
amount is null → quarantine, not into revenue
Freshness check + row-count reconcile vs full refresh
Reconcile within 0 rows → watermark advances
right.verdict: Fast AND provably equal to a full refresh

incremental-processing.caption: The redundant 3h re-read costs pennies; the silent 2% metric loss costs a mis-reported quarter. Idempotency is what makes the safe choice cheap.

incremental-processing.text: The senior tell: sizing the look-back window from the DATA, not a guess. Measure the p99 gap between created_at and _loaded_at across a month of history — if 99% of events land within 90 minutes, a 3h window is defensible and you can say so in review. 'I set it to 24h to be safe' is not caution; it is 8x the redundant work with no evidence behind the number. DORA does not define a data-quality practice; it defines delivery-performance metrics. Rephrase: 'Grounds it in SWEBOK data-quality practice: every threshold in a pipeline should trace to a measurement, not a vibe.'

incremental-processing.question: A reviewer says: 'Prove this incremental model isn't just a happy-path answer — show me it can't silently lose data.' Which evidence actually answers that?
options: The model runs in 90 seconds instead of 6 hours.

A reconciliation query showing the incremental table's row count and daily-revenue sum match a full-refresh rebuild, plus a documented look-back window sized from the observed created_at→_loaded_at lag.
The dbt run completed with no errors this morning.
The schema matches the source contract.
incremental-processing.explanation: Silent loss never throws an error and never shows up as slowness — options 1, 3, and 4 are all consistent with dropping late-arriving rows. Only option 2 proves the invariant that matters: incremental result EQUALS full refresh (reconciliation), and the mechanism that guarantees it (a look-back window sized from measured lag). That reconciliation number is the exact evidence the reviewer asked for.

incremental-processing.intro: Prove your incremental pipeline holds — no vibes:
items: Reconcile: rebuild the table as a full refresh into a temp schema and diff row count + a key metric sum against the incremental table. If they differ, your watermark or look-back is wrong — not the reconciliation.
Freshness check: confirm max(_loaded_at) in the warehouse is within your SLA of source; a stale watermark that never advanced is a failed run masquerading as success.
Late-data test: inject a row with created_at inside the look-back window but _loaded_at now, re-run, and confirm it lands exactly once (idempotent merge, no duplicate).
Quarantine: feed a malformed record (null amount) and confirm it diverts to quarantine and never moves the metric.
Look-back is justified: your window is sized from the observed created_at→_loaded_at distribution, and you can name the percentile it covers.
Failure durability: kill the run mid-load and re-run; the watermark must NOT have advanced, so no data is skipped.

prompts: In your own words: why does filtering on created_at instead of _loaded_at silently lose late-arriving data — and why doesn't a bigger watermark fix it?
Explain why an idempotent merge (unique_key) is what makes a look-back window cheap, using your own model as the example.
Your reviewer asks 'how do you know this equals a full refresh?' — walk through the exact reconciliation evidence in your packet.

incremental-processing.text: The same pattern travels to any place where you process a growing stream against a durable checkpoint: CDC replication (watermark = last committed LSN, look-back = replication lag), a streaming job's event-time watermark with allowed lateness, or a governance backfill that must re-run one partition without double-counting. What stays invariant: watermark + bounded look-back + idempotent upsert, and the reconciliation that proves incremental equals full. What changes with scale, latency, or privacy: how wide the look-back must be, whether you partition-swap instead of merge, and whether late data past the window is dropped, side-lined, or triggers a full backfill. Carry the `data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md` forward — this is the exact incremental section your data-platform capstone reuses for its DAG/model proof and quality report.

data-quality-tests.outcome: Take one real (or realistic) source table feeding a downstream metric and add Data Quality Tests that catch stale or malformed data BEFORE it corrupts that metric: a schema check, a freshness check, a bad-record quarantine, and a metric reconciliation — packaged as a reviewable artifact.
data-quality-tests.proof: data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md with five proofs wired in: schema check, freshness check, lineage map (source -> model -> metric), bad-record quarantine report, and metric reconciliation. A reviewer can run the tests, see one fail on injected bad data, and trace which metric it protected.
data-quality-tests.unlock: Your packet has a failing test on bad input, a passing test on good input, and a lineage line naming the exact metric each test defends.
data-quality-tests.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have data quality tests if every test passes green on a table you never tried to break. A suite that only says 'yes' is a green light bolted over a broken sensor. Each test must be able to FAIL loudly on stale or malformed rows — and you must have seen it fail.

data-quality-tests.text: The exec dashboard says revenue is up 12% and the board is thrilled — until someone notices the orders source stopped loading two days ago and the number is 100% stale. No pipeline error fired. The data was late, not wrong-shaped, so nothing caught it.

This lesson opens Module 3 (Quality) — the point where your pipeline stops trusting its own inputs. Data quality tests sit on the edges between source contract, warehouse, and metric, turning 'the load ran' into 'the data is correct, fresh, and traceable to the number it feeds.'

data-quality-tests.prompt: Your nightly dbt run finishes green — every model built, zero errors. Is your revenue metric trustworthy this morning? Decide before reading on.
data-quality-tests.reveal: No — a green build only proves SQL compiled and ran, not that the data is correct. The source can be a full day stale, a currency column can arrive as text, duplicate order rows can double-count — all while every model builds cleanly. 'The pipeline ran' and 'the data is right' are different claims. Data quality tests assert the second one, which the orchestrator never checks for you.

data-quality-tests.title: A data quality test is a falsifiable assertion on the data, not the pipeline
data-quality-tests.text: Assert what MUST be true of the data — shape (schema), timeliness (freshness), validity (constraints) — as a check that FAILS on violation and quarantines the bad rows before they reach a metric. The invariant: it must be able to fail on real bad data.

data-quality-tests.title: Where the four tests guard the pipeline
data-quality-tests.subtitle: Source -> warehouse -> dbt model -> metric. Each test is a gate; the quarantine catches bad rows before they reach the number. Failure path (stale/malformed) is marked in warning; the repaired path in success.

data-quality-tests.title: Writing the tests: dbt schema + freshness + a validity constraint
data-quality-tests.subtitle: The real artifact — dbt source contract with tests that FAIL on stale or malformed orders data.
data-quality-tests.code:
version: 2
sources:
  - name: raw
    tables:
      - name: orders
        # freshness: fail the run if the newest row is > 6h old
        loaded_at_field: loaded_at
        freshness:
          warn_after: {count: 3, period: hour}
          error_after: {count: 6, period: hour}
        columns:
          - name: order_id
            tests: [unique, not_null]        # no dupes, no missing keys
          - name: amount_usd
            tests:
              - not_null
              - dbt_utils.accepted_range:     # amount must be a positive number
                  min_value: 0
          - name: currency
            tests:
              - accepted_values: {values: ['USD','EUR','GBP']}

steps.label: The freshness check
steps.note: loaded_at_field + error_after makes staleness a hard failure. This is the exact gap in the mission: data that is late but well-formed. 6h past the SLA and `dbt source freshness` errors — the run stops before the stale batch feeds the metric.

steps.label: Key integrity (schema)
steps.note: unique + not_null on order_id. A duplicated order row double-counts revenue; a null key breaks the join to fct_orders. Both fail here, not silently in the dashboard.

steps.label: Value validity
steps.note: amount_usd not_null AND non-negative. A refund arriving as a positive charge, or a NULL amount summed as zero, is a malformed record — accepted_range catches it before reconciliation.

steps.label: Enum validity
steps.note: currency must be a known code. 'usd' lowercased, or a junk value from a bad upstream deploy, fails accepted_values instead of quietly corrupting a multi-currency total.

steps.label: warn vs error
steps.note: warn_after at 3h pages nobody but shows yellow; error_after at 6h halts the pipeline. The tradeoff you defend in review: how stale is tolerable before you stop serving the number at all.

data-quality-tests.caption: Run `dbt test` + `dbt source freshness`: inject a row with amount_usd = -5 or hold the load 7h and the suite goes RED — that red is the whole point.

data-quality-tests.title: Weak 'tests' vs a real quality suite
data-quality-tests.subtitle: Same orders table feeding the same revenue metric. Only one can catch the stale-data incident from the mission.

left.label: Weak: the pipeline ran, so ship it

No freshness field — stale load looks identical to fresh
No row-level constraints (nulls, dupes, bad currency pass)
Bad rows flow straight into fct_orders
No lineage — nobody knows which metric a failure hits
left.verdict: Green build over a stale, double-counted number

right.label: Gold: falsifiable assertions on the data
lines: Freshness SLA (error_after 6h) halts on stale batches
unique/not_null/accepted_range/accepted_values on the source
Malformed rows land in a quarantine table with a report
Metric reconciliation: sum(fct_orders) == sum(raw valid)
Lineage names it: this test defends `revenue_daily`
right.verdict: Caught, quarantined, and traced to the metric

data-quality-tests.caption: The difference is falsifiability. A suite you have watched go RED on injected bad data is evidence; a permanently-green one is decoration.

data-quality-tests.text: The senior tell: test the DATA, not just the SQL. Juniors assert 'the model compiled'; seniors assert 'the newest row is < 6h old AND the total reconciles to source.' Freshness is the test everyone skips and the one that catches the incident that never throws an error — late data is silently wrong data.

data-quality-tests.question: A reviewer says: 'Your test suite is all green — prove this isn't just a happy-path answer.' What is the strongest evidence?
options: The dbt run finished with zero errors last night.
You show a quarantine report + a screenshot of the suite going RED when you injected a stale batch and a negative amount, plus a lineage line naming the metric each test protects.
There are 40 tests in the YAML file.
The dashboard number looks about right compared to last week.
data-quality-tests.explanation: Evidence of quality testing is proof the tests can FAIL and that you have seen them fail on realistic bad data — the injected stale batch and negative amount — plus the quarantine artifact and the lineage tying each check to the metric it defends. A green run (1), a high test count (3), and a plausible-looking number (4) are exactly the happy-path signals the reviewer is challenging.

data-quality-tests.intro: Prove the suite is real — no green-by-default:
items: Schema check: inject a duplicate order_id and a NULL amount_usd — the unique/not_null tests must go RED. If they stay green, the test isn't wired to the source.
Freshness check: hold the load past error_after (or backdate loaded_at 7h) — `dbt source freshness` must ERROR, not warn-and-continue.
Quarantine: confirm the malformed rows actually land in a dead-letter/quarantine table with a count, not just get dropped silently.
Lineage map: for each test, name the exact downstream metric it defends (source -> fct_orders -> revenue_daily). A test with no named metric is untraceable.
Metric reconciliation: sum of the clean model equals sum of valid source rows for the window — and the delta is exactly the quarantined bad rows, not a mystery.

Explain freshness vs schema tests using your own source: which incident does each one catch, and why does the mission's stale-data bug slip past schema alone?
Walk the lineage: name the exact path from your source table to the metric, and say which test defends which edge.

data-quality-tests.text: The same pattern travels to any new source, schema-drift case, or late-arriving-data problem — what stays invariant is 'assert the data, make it falsifiable, quarantine, reconcile, trace to the metric'; what changes is the SLA and constraints. A streaming clickstream needs a tighter freshness window and watermark handling for late events; a third-party API feed needs stricter schema tests because you don't control its shape; a GDPR-governed table adds a validity test that no PII column leaks past the boundary. This is the exact artifact your capstone reuses: data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md becomes the quality + lineage evidence in the data platform capstone's contracts, DAG/model proof, quality report, and runbook — the portfolio claim is not 'I know dbt tests,' it's 'here is a metric I proved fresh, valid, quarantined, and reconciled.'

reconciliation.outcome: Take one real pipeline where a source table feeds a downstream metric, and build the Reconciliation section of data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md: the count/sum that MUST tie between source and warehouse, the tolerance, the freshness bound, and the quarantine rule for records that fail — then run it once and capture the reconciliation report showing what passed, what failed, and what got quarantined.
reconciliation.proof: The Reconciliation section of data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md: a named source-to-target tie-out (row count and a control total), an explicit tolerance and freshness SLA, a bad-record quarantine report, and a metric reconciliation line. A reviewer can point at the number that proves source and warehouse agree — not a claim that they do.
reconciliation.unlock: Your packet names the reconciliation invariant, sets a tolerance and freshness bound, quarantines bad records instead of dropping them, and shows a report where the numbers tie.
reconciliation.doNotClaim: Do not claim the data is 'reconciled' because the dbt model ran green. A model that runs is not a model that ties. Reconciliation is a NUMBER that matches (or matches within tolerance) across the source contract and the warehouse — with the mismatched rows quarantined and counted, not silently dropped.

reconciliation.text: The revenue dashboard reads $2.4M on Monday and the finance team builds the board deck on it. The upstream orders extract silently truncated at 850k of 1.1M rows on Sunday night, every dbt model ran green, and no test failed — because nobody reconciled the warehouse count back to the source. The metric was wrong for three days before a human noticed the number 'felt low.'

Reconciliation is the control that catches stale or malformed source data BEFORE it corrupts a downstream metric — the tie-out between what the source contract promised and what actually landed in the warehouse. It is Section 5 of the data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet you carry through this module, and it is the difference between a pipeline that runs and a pipeline you can trust a board number to.

reconciliation.prompt: Your dbt build is fully green: every model compiled, every not_null and unique test passed. Is the daily revenue metric trustworthy? Answer before reading on.
reconciliation.reveal: No — green tests prove the data is well-FORMED, not COMPLETE or FRESH. not_null and unique validate the rows that arrived; they say nothing about the rows that didn't. If the source extract dropped 250k orders or landed 6 hours stale, every column-level test still passes and the metric is quietly wrong. Reconciliation is the one control that compares a total against the source of truth, so 'missing 23% of rows' becomes a failure instead of a smaller-but-plausible number.

reconciliation.title: Reconciliation ties a control total across the boundary, within a tolerance, or quarantines
reconciliation.text: The invariant: a source count or sum must equal the warehouse count or sum, within a declared tolerance and freshness bound. On a break, quarantine the offending records and fail loudly — never let a silently-short metric ship.

reconciliation.title: The reconciliation query, one line at a time
reconciliation.subtitle: The real tie-out from data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md — source control total vs warehouse, with tolerance, freshness, and a quarantine count. Fails the build when it breaks.
reconciliation.code:
-- Section 5: Reconciliation — orders_daily source-of-truth tie-out
with src as (   -- source contract: control totals pulled from the system of record
  select count(*) as src_rows, sum(amount) as src_amount, max(created_at) as src_max_ts
  from raw_orders where order_date = '{{ run_date }}'
),
wh as (         -- warehouse: what actually landed in the staged model
  select count(*) as wh_rows, sum(amount) as wh_amount, max(loaded_at) as wh_max_ts
  from stg_orders where order_date = '{{ run_date }}'
),
quar as (       -- quarantine: malformed rows held aside, NOT dropped
  select count(*) as bad_rows from raw_orders_quarantine where order_date = '{{ run_date }}'
)
select
  src.src_rows, wh.wh_rows, quar.bad_rows,
  abs(src.src_amount - wh.wh_amount) as amount_delta,
  -- INVARIANT 1: row counts tie once quarantined rows are accounted for
  (src.src_rows = wh.wh_rows + quar.bad_rows) as rows_tie,
  -- INVARIANT 2: control total ties within a 0.01 tolerance (float drift only)
  (abs(src.src_amount - wh.wh_amount) <= 0.01) as amount_ties,
  -- INVARIANT 3: freshness — warehouse partition is no more than 2h behind source
  (wh.wh_max_ts >= src.src_max_ts - interval '2 hours') as is_fresh
from src, wh, quar

steps.note: The source of truth answers the only questions that matter for a metric: how many rows, what is the sum, and how fresh. Never reconcile against another warehouse table — reconcile against the system of record.

steps.label: Invariant 2 — control total ties within tolerance
steps.note: sum(amount) must match within 0.01. Tolerance exists for float drift, NOT for missing rows — a tolerance wide enough to hide dropped orders is decoration.

steps.label: Invariant 3 — freshness bound
steps.note: The warehouse partition must be within 2h of the source's newest timestamp. Stale-but-complete is still wrong for a daily metric; freshness is a first-class reconciliation check, not an afterthought.

reconciliation.text: The same control travels to every boundary where data crosses a trust line. A new source? Tie its control total to its system of record before you build a single metric on it. A schema-drift case — the source renames amount to gross_amount? Your sum stops tying and the reconcile gate fails loudly instead of the metric quietly zeroing. Late-arriving data? The freshness bound and partition-level tie-out are exactly what let you accept it as a backfill instead of mistaking it for loss. What stays invariant is the move: compare a total across the boundary, within a declared tolerance, and quarantine the mismatch. What changes is the tolerance, the freshness bound, and the control total you choose — tighter for financial metrics, looser for best-effort analytics. This reconciliation section is the piece of data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md the capstone reuses unchanged: the proof that your data product's numbers tie to the source, not just that the pipeline ran green.

One analyst opens twelve tabs and starts guessing; the other opens the lineage packet, traces revenue back through the dbt model to a source table whose freshness check went red at 2 a.m., and names the culprit in ninety seconds. backfills-reprocessing.doNotClaim: Do not claim a backfill is complete because the job exited 0. A green exit that appended a second copy of every row, or silently dropped records that failed the schema check, is a corrupted metric wearing a success badge. The proof is reconciliation against the source of truth, not the exit code.

backfills-reprocessing.text: Finance opens the revenue dashboard and last Tuesday is 2.3x too high. A late vendor file re-landed overnight, the pipeline appended it on top of the old partition, and now every downstream dbt model, every lineage-linked metric, and the board deck all inherit the double-count. The fix is not "re-run the job" — it is a surgical backfill that replaces exactly that partition and proves the number is right again.

In the production-pressure phase, data is never write-once: source contracts get corrected, late-arriving events land after the partition closed, and schema drift forces reprocessing of history. Backfills reprocessing is how you rewrite a bounded slice of the warehouse without corrupting the rest — and it only counts when lineage and reconciliation prove the downstream metric recovered.

backfills-reprocessing.prompt: A partition landed with bad data. Your instinct: re-run the pipeline so it reprocesses that day and appends the corrected rows. Before you do — what breaks? Answer first.
backfills-reprocessing.reveal: You just doubled the partition. An append-mode reprocess adds the corrected rows next to the wrong ones — now the metric sums both. The invariant of a backfill is idempotent replacement: reprocessing partition 2026-06-24 must overwrite that partition's rows so the result is identical whether you run it once or five times. "Re-run" is not "backfill" until the write is partition-scoped and idempotent. The number being wrong is bad; being non-deterministically wrong on every retry is unrecoverable.

backfills-reprocessing.title: A backfill is an idempotent, partition-scoped replace — proven by reconciliation
backfills-reprocessing.text: Reprocess a bounded partition window by overwriting, never appending, so N runs equal one run. The invariant: same input, same partition, same warehouse state. It is done only when the reprocessed metric reconciles against the source contract — exit code is not proof.

backfills-reprocessing.title: The idempotent backfill — scope, quarantine, replace, reconcile
backfills-reprocessing.subtitle: A partition-scoped reprocess. Every line is a forcing function: append is banned, bad records are quarantined not dropped, and the run fails unless the metric reconciles.
backfills-reprocessing.code:
# Backfill: reprocess ONE partition, idempotently, with proof.
PARTITION = "2026-06-24"          # bounded window, not "all of history"
RECON_TOLERANCE = 0.005          # 0.5% drift allowed vs source of truth

def backfill(partition: str) -> None:
    raw = read_source(partition)                      # re-read corrected vendor file
    good, bad = split_on_contract(raw)                # schema + freshness check
    write_quarantine(bad, partition)                  # divert bad rows, never drop

    # IDEMPOTENT: delete the partition, then insert. N runs == 1 run.
    warehouse.delete_partition("revenue_daily", partition)
    warehouse.insert("revenue_daily", good, partition=partition)

    dbt_run(models=["revenue_daily"], partition=partition)  # rebuild downstream

    # PROOF: reconcile the reprocessed metric against the source contract.
    src_total = source_revenue_total(partition)
    wh_total = warehouse_metric_total("revenue_daily", partition)
    drift = abs(wh_total - src_total) / src_total
    if drift > RECON_TOLERANCE:
        raise BackfillNotReconciled(partition, drift, src_total, wh_total)

steps.label: Bound the window
steps.note: One partition and a reconciliation tolerance. "Backfill everything" is not a plan — it is a way to turn a one-day problem into a month-long outage. Scope is the first safety property.

steps.label: Contract-gate, then quarantine
steps.note: split_on_contract enforces schema + freshness. Bad rows go to a quarantine store you can inspect — dropping them silently is how a partial partition passes as complete.

steps.label: Delete then insert — the idempotency core
steps.note: This is the whole skill. delete_partition + insert makes the write replace, so re-running produces identical warehouse state. An append here is the double-count bug from the mission.

steps.label: Rebuild only the affected lineage
steps.note: Reprocessing the raw partition is not enough — the dbt models built on it still hold the old numbers. Rebuild the downstream models scoped to the same partition.

steps.label: Reconcile or fail loudly
steps.note: The metric must match the source of truth within tolerance. Raising BackfillNotReconciled is the point: a backfill that cannot prove the number recovered must NOT report success.
