Exit code (1), a plain re-run (3, which is exactly the double-count trap), and eyeballing (4) are happy-path claims with no proof.

items: Idempotency: run the backfill twice and diff warehouse row counts + the metric total. If run 2 differs from run 1, your write appends instead of replaces — fix it before anything else.
Scope: the partition window is bounded and named. If you cannot state the exact partitions touched, you cannot state the blast radius.
Quarantine: bad records are diverted to an inspectable store WITH a count, never silently dropped. A partition that discarded failures is not complete.
Lineage rebuild: every dbt model downstream of the reprocessed partition was rebuilt scoped to that partition — not just the raw table.
Reconciliation: the reprocessed metric matches the source contract within a stated tolerance, and the backfill FAILS loudly if it does not.

prompts: In your own words: why does append-mode reprocessing turn a recoverable bad partition into an unrecoverable one, and how does delete+insert fix it?
Explain to a teammate why quarantining bad records (with a count) beats dropping them — using freshness and completeness of the partition in your answer.
Which single number in your packet proves the metric recovered, and where does that number come from relative to the source contract?

backfills-reprocessing.text: The same pattern travels to every reprocessing case: schema drift (a column type changed — reprocess only the affected partitions, idempotently, reconcile), a new late-arriving-data window (backfill the partitions the event should have landed in), or a governance-driven correction (a PII field must be re-masked across history). What stays invariant: bounded scope, idempotent replace, quarantine over drop, and reconciliation against the source of truth. What changes with scale and cost: how you window the partitions (one day vs. a year), whether you throttle to protect the live warehouse, and how tight the reconciliation tolerance must be for the metric's audience. This same data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md is the artifact your data-platform capstone reuses — the backfill section, the quarantine report, and the reconciliation number are the evidence that proves the pipeline is operable under correction, not just on the happy path.

streaming-event-data.outcome: Take one real (or realistic) event stream feeding a metric, and build the data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md for it: the source contract (event schema + freshness SLA), the quality gate that quarantines bad records before they reach the warehouse, and the lineage map from raw event to the metric it powers.
streaming-event-data.proof: data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md with: a versioned event contract (required fields + types + freshness SLA), a quality gate that quarantines schema-invalid and stale records, a lineage map (event -> raw -> staging -> mart -> metric), and a metric-reconciliation check. A reviewer can trace one event from ingestion to the dashboard number and see exactly where a bad record gets stopped.
streaming-event-data.unlock: Your packet names the contract, quarantines bad records at the boundary, and traces lineage end-to-end from event to metric.
streaming-event-data.doNotClaim: Do not claim you handle streaming event data if your pipeline lets a malformed or stale event flow straight into the metric. 'It loaded without erroring' is not proof — a silently corrupted metric is the exact failure this skill exists to prevent. The contract must be able to REJECT an event, or it is decoration.

streaming-event-data.text: At 9:14 a.m. a mobile SDK ships a new build that renames purchase_cents to amount_cents. No pipeline errors. By noon the revenue dashboard reads $0 for the day, the VP is in the channel, and nobody can say when it broke or which numbers to trust — because the event stream had no contract standing at the door.

Streaming event data is the rawest, least-trustworthy source in a data platform: high-volume, schema-drifting, arriving late and out of order, straight from clients you do not control. This is the production-pressure lesson where a source contract, a quality gate, and lineage stop one bad event from silently corrupting a metric everyone trusts.

streaming-event-data.prompt: An event stream feeds your daily revenue metric. To make it trustworthy, where do you enforce correctness — at the warehouse where you compute the metric, or somewhere else? Decide before reading.
streaming-event-data.reveal: At the boundary, the moment the event lands — not at the metric. If you only validate at the warehouse, a malformed event has already been written, joined, and aggregated before anything complains; the corruption is downstream and invisible. The invariant of streaming event data: validate against a contract at ingestion and quarantine what fails, so bad records never enter the lineage that produces the number. You cannot un-poison a metric after the fact — you keep the poison out of the pipeline.

streaming-event-data.title: A source contract quarantines bad events at the boundary, and lineage proves where each one went
streaming-event-data.text: Define the event's required fields, types, and freshness SLA as a versioned contract. At ingestion, valid records pass to the warehouse; schema-invalid or stale records are quarantined, not dropped. Lineage traces every event from raw to metric so any number is auditable.

streaming-event-data.title: The streaming event pipeline — contract at the door, quarantine on the side
streaming-event-data.subtitle: Events hit a quality gate FIRST. Valid records flow raw -> staging -> mart -> the revenue metric; schema-invalid and stale records divert to a quarantine store. The dead-letter path and the clean lineage are both visible — this is the failure path and the repair path in one picture.

steps.note: purchase.v2 is explicit. When the SDK renames purchase_cents, events no longer satisfy v2 and get caught — instead of silently writing NULL revenue. A versioned contract turns a silent drift into a loud, contained failure.

steps.note: Not just 'is it well-formed' but 'is it recent enough to trust'. Late-arriving events past the SLA are stale for the live metric — they go to quarantine, not into today's number.

steps.label: Schema check quarantines, does not crash
steps.note: A missing or wrong-typed field returns quarantine with a reason string — the bad record is HELD for autopsy and replay, never dropped and never let through. Dropping loses evidence; letting through corrupts the metric.

steps.label: Freshness check runs after schema
steps.note: Order matters: you cannot judge freshness on an event missing event_ts. Schema first, then freshness — the cheapest disqualifier first.

steps.label: 'pass' is the only door into lineage
steps.note: This return is the invariant made code: only a record that satisfies the full contract enters raw landing and therefore the lineage that produces the metric. Everything else is quarantined with a reason.

streaming-event-data.caption: The gold move is not 'more validation everywhere' — it is one contract at the door plus lineage behind it, so a bad event is stopped once and every number stays traceable.

streaming-event-data.text: The senior tell in streaming: they quarantine, they never silently drop. Dropping a malformed event makes the pipeline look green while destroying the evidence you need to explain the gap and replay it after the fix. A held bad record with a reason string is a diagnosis; a dropped one is a mystery. DORA does not address event handling or malformed-event discipline. Rephrase: 'This is CS2023 discipline — treat late and malformed events as expected states with a defined path, not exceptions you swallow.' Only cite DORA 2024 as an anchor where the point is a delivery-performance metric (deploy frequency, lead time, change-failure rate, recovery time); do not anchor implementation-technique claims to DORA.

streaming-event-data.question: A reviewer asks: 'Show me the exact evidence that your streaming pipeline is not just a happy-path answer.' Which single piece of evidence best proves it?
options: A screenshot of the dashboard showing a revenue number that looks reasonable.
A quarantine/dead-letter report showing malformed and stale events were caught at the boundary with reasons, plus a lineage map tracing a valid event to the metric it feeds.
A note saying the pipeline ran overnight without throwing an error.
A statement that the event schema is documented in the team wiki.
streaming-event-data.explanation: Happy-path pipelines also produce reasonable-looking numbers (1) and run without errors (3) — right up until a silent drift corrupts them. The proof that streaming event data is handled is that the pipeline can CATCH a bad event (the quarantine report with reasons) and TRACE a good one (lineage to the metric). Documentation alone (4) proves intent, not behavior. Only option 2 shows the failure path being handled and the number being auditable.

streaming-event-data.intro: Prove your packet holds under production pressure — no vibes:
items: Schema check: feed a malformed event (missing/renamed required field) through the gate. It must be quarantined with a reason, not written to raw landing.
Freshness check: feed an event older than the SLA. It must divert to quarantine, not into the live metric's partition.
Quarantine report: confirm bad records are HELD with their reason (schema vs freshness), not silently dropped — you can list them and replay them after a fix.
Lineage map: pick one number on the metric and trace it back through mart -> staging -> raw -> the specific raw events. If you cannot, the lineage is incomplete.
Metric reconciliation: compare the metric's total against the sum of valid raw events for the window. A gap must be explainable by the quarantine count, not a mystery.

prompts: In your own words: why does validating a streaming event at the warehouse (instead of the ingestion boundary) let a bad event corrupt the metric before anything complains?
Explain the difference between DROPPING a malformed event and QUARANTINING it, using your own quality gate as the example. What does quarantine let you do that dropping does not?
Trace one number on your metric back to its raw events out loud. Where in that lineage would a schema drift or a late-arriving event get caught?

streaming-event-data.text: Same pattern, any streaming source with an untrusted producer. Swap the purchase SDK for IoT sensor telemetry, clickstream events, or a third-party webhook: the contract, freshness SLA, boundary quarantine, and lineage all stay invariant — what changes is the required fields, the SLA window (sub-second for sensors, hours for batch webhooks), and how you handle late-arriving data (watermarks and reprocessing windows instead of a hard stale-drop). Carry data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md straight into the course capstone: it is the reusable evidence that turns 'I understand streaming ingestion' into 'here is a contract that quarantined a real bad event and a lineage that made the metric auditable — read it.' A metric is only as trustworthy as the door its events walked through.

warehouse-performance.outcome: Take one real (or realistic) warehouse table whose query is slow or whose cost is climbing, and build the data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md: name the hot query, the partition/cluster key you chose, the rejected layout, the freshness + data-quality checks that gate it, and the before/after scan proof. Not a note — a reviewable artifact for the pipeline.
warehouse-performance.proof: data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md with: the hot query + its filter predicate, the chosen partition/cluster key, the rejected layout with why, an EXPLAIN or bytes-scanned before/after (e.g. 480 GB → 12 GB), a freshness check, a bad-record quarantine line, and a lineage note tying it to the downstream metric. A reviewer reads the before/after scan and agrees the layout — not luck — caused the drop.
warehouse-performance.unlock: Your packet names the hot query's predicate, the partition/cluster key that serves it, the rejected layout, and a measured before/after scan — with a freshness + quality gate attached.
warehouse-performance.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'tuned the warehouse' from a faster wall-clock alone. Wall-clock moves with warehouse load and cache. The proof is bytes/partitions SCANNED dropping because the layout matches the predicate. A query that got faster because the result was cached is a mirage, not a tuning.

warehouse-performance.text: The exec dashboard timed out at the board meeting, the finance metric was six hours stale, and the bill for that one table crossed five figures last month — all three trace to a single design choice nobody wrote down: how the warehouse table is laid out versus how it is actually queried.

This is the production-pressure phase of the data platform: a table that was fine at a gigabyte melts a query planner at a terabyte. Warehouse performance is where source contract, freshness, lineage, and cost stop being separate concerns and become one design — the layout that serves the metric without scanning the whole history.

warehouse-performance.prompt: Your dashboard query filters `WHERE event_date = '2026-06-30'` and it scans the entire 2 TB table every run. The table has a b-tree index on event_date. Why is it still reading everything? Answer before reading on.
warehouse-performance.reveal: An OLTP index doesn't save you in a columnar warehouse — the warehouse decides what to read by PARTITION and file min/max stats, not a b-tree. If the table isn't partitioned on event_date, every file could contain that date, so the planner must open all of them. The fix isn't an index; it's physical layout: partition (or cluster) on the column your hot query filters, so the planner prunes 99% of files before reading a byte. Indexes tune row lookups; partitioning tunes scans — and warehouses live and die on scans.

warehouse-performance.title: Lay the table out for the predicate — prune before you read
warehouse-performance.text: Warehouse cost is bytes scanned. Partition (coarse) and cluster/sort (fine) on the columns your hot query filters, so the planner prunes files by min/max stats before reading. The invariant: layout must match the predicate, or every query pays for the whole table.

warehouse-performance.title: The scan path: where partition pruning kills or saves the query
warehouse-performance.subtitle: Same query, two layouts. Unpartitioned → planner must read every file (full scan, stale-prone, 480 GB). Partitioned on event_date + clustered on customer_id → prune to one partition (12 GB). The freshness gate blocks a stale metric before it reaches the dashboard.

warehouse-performance.title: The layout + the gates that make it trustworthy (dbt model)
warehouse-performance.subtitle: The real artifact: a dbt model config that partitions and clusters for the hot predicate, plus the freshness + quality tests that gate it. This is what goes in the packet.
warehouse-performance.code:
{{
  config(
    materialized='incremental',
    incremental_strategy='insert_overwrite',
    partition_by={'field': 'event_date', 'data_type': 'date'},
    cluster_by=['customer_id'],
    on_schema_change='fail'
  )
}}

select
    event_date,
    customer_id,
    sum(amount) as revenue
from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
where amount >= 0                       -- quarantine malformed negatives
{% if is_incremental() %}
  and event_date > (select max(event_date) from {{ this }})
{% endif %}
group by event_date, customer_id

-- schema.yml (the contract + proof gates)
-- tests:
--   - dbt_utils.recency: {datepart: hour, field: event_date, interval: 26}  # freshness SLA
--   - not_null: [event_date, customer_id, revenue]                          # data quality
--   - dbt_utils.accepted_range: {column: revenue, min_value: 0}             # bad-record guard

steps.label: Partition on the hot predicate
steps.note: The dashboard filters event_date, so partition on event_date. Now the planner prunes to one day's files instead of the whole table — the 480 GB → 12 GB drop lives here.

steps.label: Cluster on the second filter
steps.note: Within a partition, sort by customer_id so per-customer queries read a contiguous slice, not the whole day. Partition = coarse prune; cluster = fine prune.

steps.label: insert_overwrite, not full rebuild
steps.note: Incremental with partition overwrite reprocesses only changed partitions. A full rebuild every run is the cost leak that looks like a 'slow warehouse'.

steps.label: Quarantine at the source
steps.note: amount >= 0 keeps malformed negatives out of the metric. A bad record that reaches revenue is a wrong number on a board slide — quarantine beats reconcile-after.

steps.label: Only scan new partitions
steps.note: The incremental predicate means the build itself prunes — you tune the pipeline's own cost, not just the reader's.

steps.label: The proof gates
steps.note: Freshness (recency), completeness (not_null), and range checks. These are the 'schema check + freshness check + bad-record quarantine' the answer key demands — the packet's evidence.

warehouse-performance.caption: Run once: unpartitioned EXPLAIN shows 480 GB scanned; after this config, the same dashboard query shows 12 GB and the recency test guards staleness. Paste both into the packet — the delta is the proof.

warehouse-performance.subtitle: Both return the correct number today. Only one survives the next 10x of data.

warehouse-performance.caption: The tell isn't speed on a small table — both are fast at a gigabyte. It's what happens at a terabyte: the weak table's scan and cost grow with total history; the gold table's grow only with the day you query.

warehouse-performance.text: Senior data engineers tune to the QUERY, not the table. Before choosing a partition key, they read the actual WHERE clauses in the query logs and partition on the column that appears most in filters — high-cardinality columns like user_id become cluster keys, low-cardinality time columns become partitions. Partitioning on a column nobody filters on is cost with no benefit; it's the most common self-inflicted warehouse bill.

warehouse-performance.question: A reviewer asks for the exact evidence that your table is tuned, not just lucky. Which artifact proves it?
options: The dashboard 'feels faster' since you deployed the change.
A before/after EXPLAIN showing bytes scanned dropped from 480 GB to 12 GB for the hot query, because its filter now matches the partition/cluster key — plus a passing freshness test.
The table now has an index on event_date.
The query returned in 0.4 seconds on your last run.
warehouse-performance.explanation: Only option 2 isolates the cause: bytes SCANNED fell because the planner can prune to the predicate's partition — that is layout, not caching or warehouse load. 'Feels faster' (0) and a single fast run (3) can both be cache hits or a quiet warehouse. An index (2 in the list) is an OLTP reflex that a columnar planner ignores for scans. Bytes-scanned before/after is the one number a reviewer can't argue with.

warehouse-performance.intro: Prove the tuning holds — bytes, not vibes:
items: Run EXPLAIN (or the dry-run byte estimate) on the hot query BEFORE and AFTER the layout change. If bytes scanned didn't drop, the partition key doesn't match the predicate — fix the key, not the query.
Confirm your partition key is a column that actually appears in the query's WHERE clause. Partitioning on an unfiltered column scans just as much.
Run the freshness (recency) test and force it to FAIL once (hold back a partition) — a check that can only pass is theater. It must be able to say 'stale'.
Feed one malformed record (a negative amount) and confirm it lands in quarantine, not in the metric. The reconciliation number must be unchanged.
Trace the lineage in the packet end to end: source table → this model → the dashboard metric. If you can't name every hop, you can't name the blast radius when it breaks.

prompts: In your own words: why does a b-tree index help an OLTP row lookup but do nothing for a warehouse full-table scan — and what replaces it?
Explain the difference between a partition key and a cluster key using YOUR table's hot query as the example. Which column got which, and why?
Your before/after showed 480 GB → 12 GB. Explain to a skeptic why that drop is the layout and not a lucky cache hit — what would you point to?

warehouse-performance.text: The pattern is invariant: read the real access pattern, lay the data out to serve it, prove it by what got pruned, and gate freshness + quality so a fast-but-wrong answer can't ship. It transfers the moment the context changes — a late-arriving-data source means your partition-overwrite must reprocess yesterday's partition, not just today's; a schema-drift source means on_schema_change='fail' turns a silent corruption into a loud stop; a streaming source swaps date partitions for hourly ones. What stays constant: layout matches predicate, and the proof is bytes pruned. What changes: the grain of the partition and which failure you gate hardest. Carry the data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md into the capstone — it's the same artifact the contracts/DAG-proof/quality-report/runbook build reuses, and the portfolio claim is not 'I understand warehouse performance' but 'here is a table I laid out for its hot query, cut its scan 40x, and gated its freshness — read the before/after.'

privacy-governance.outcome: Take one real (or realistic) data product pipeline and attach a Privacy Governance layer: classify every column by sensitivity, declare the masking/access policy in the source contract, and prove lineage carries the PII tag from source to the served metric. The output is a reviewable artifact, not a note.
privacy-governance.proof: Section added to data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md: a column-level PII classification, a policy per class (mask | tokenize | drop | allow), a lineage map showing the tag propagating source → warehouse → dbt model → metric, and a quarantine report proving one unclassified column was BLOCKED before it reached the mart. A reviewer can point to the exact column that would have leaked.
privacy-governance.unlock: Every column in the contract has a sensitivity class, each class has an enforced policy, and lineage proves the PII tag survives every hop to the served metric.
privacy-governance.doNotClaim: Do not claim "the pipeline is governed" because you wrote a data-handling paragraph. Governance that lives only in a doc is theater — the invariant is enforcement in the pipeline. If an unclassified column can still flow to the mart, you have a policy nobody obeys.

privacy-governance.text: A dbt model ships a new analytics table on Friday. Monday, someone notices raw_email and a home ZIP sitting in a dashboard three teams can query — nobody classified the column, so the pipeline copied it straight through. The fix is not a policy PDF; it is a tag that travels with the data and a gate that stops the untagged.
privacy-governance.callback: You already framed the pipeline, routed the diagnosis, and mapped the system — now you govern what flows through it.

privacy-governance.text: In the production-pressure phase, a pipeline is not done when the metric is correct — it is done when the metric is correct AND provably safe. Privacy Governance is the layer that makes "who can see which column, and how do we know" a property of the pipeline, not a promise in a wiki.

privacy-governance.prompt: Your dbt model does SELECT * FROM raw_users to build a clean users table. The source is trusted and the tests pass. What is the privacy problem hiding in that one line? Answer before reading on.
privacy-governance.reveal: SELECT * is a governance blind spot. It copies every column — including tomorrow's new email, phone, or SSN column the source team adds without telling you — straight into the warehouse with no classification and no policy. Governance breaks silently: nothing fails, the metric is right, and PII quietly spreads to every downstream consumer. The invariant is that no column reaches a mart without a declared sensitivity class; SELECT * violates it by construction.

privacy-governance.title: Govern the column, not the document — classify, enforce, and carry the tag
privacy-governance.text: Every column gets a sensitivity class in the source contract; each class has an enforced policy (mask, tokenize, drop, allow); and lineage carries that tag to every metric. The invariant: no unclassified column reaches a mart. Policy that isn't enforced in the pipeline is decoration.

privacy-governance.title: The PII tag traveling the pipeline — failure path vs repair path
privacy-governance.subtitle: Source contract classifies each column; the governance gate BLOCKS anything unclassified. Top path (ungoverned SELECT *) leaks raw_email to the mart; bottom path masks it and carries the PII tag to the served metric.

legend.label: repair path — policy enforced, tag carried

privacy-governance.title: Writing the governance layer into the data contract
privacy-governance.subtitle: The real artifact: column-level classification + enforced policy + a gate that fails the build on any unclassified column.

steps.label: Classify every column
steps.note: Each column gets a sensitivity class. pii_direct identifies a person outright (email); pii_quasi re-identifies in combination (ZIP). No column is left without a class — that is the whole invariant.

steps.label: Direct PII → mask
steps.note: email is pii_direct, so its policy is mask (irreversible hash). A metric never needs the raw value — only whether two rows share one.

steps.label: Quasi-identifier → tokenize
steps.note: home_zip alone is not a name, but ZIP + age + gender re-identifies. Tokenize into a k-anonymity bucket so the analytic value survives and the person does not.

steps.label: The gate detects drift
steps.note: When the source team adds a column tomorrow, source_cols has it but the contract does not — unclassified is non-empty. This is the SELECT * leak, caught.

steps.label: Fail the build, do not warn
steps.note: raise, not log. A warning is ignored at 2 a.m.; a raised GovernanceError stops the run and quarantines the batch before it reaches the mart.

steps.label: Emit the enforced plan
steps.note: The gate returns the policy per column — the plan dbt applies and lineage carries. This plan IS the reviewable evidence: policy that runs, not policy that's promised.

privacy-governance.caption: Run it against a source that grew a new phone column: the gate raises BLOCKED before a single PII row lands — the failure the mission described, prevented.

privacy-governance.title: Two ways to "handle privacy" in the same pipeline
privacy-governance.subtitle: Both mention privacy. Only one changes what the pipeline actually does with an unclassified column.

privacy-governance.caption: The tell: hand a reviewer a source that grew a new column. The prose version leaks it; the enforced version fails the build and can point to the exact column it stopped.

privacy-governance.text: DORA 2024 does not state that elite teams treat governance as a build gate; that is not a DORA finding. Rephrase without DORA attribution: 'Treat governance as a build gate, not a review meeting — the same discipline that makes deploys safe makes data safe.' The senior tell is column-level lineage: not "this table has PII" but "this metric is derived from email, masked here, and here is the query that proves the raw value never left staging." A reviewer trusts the tag they can trace, not the promise they're told.

privacy-governance.question: A reviewer says: "Show me the exact evidence that this pipeline is governed, not just documented." Which response actually proves it?
options: "Our data-handling policy page says all PII is protected and the team is trained."

"Column-level lineage shows email is classed pii_direct, masked in staging, and the query proves the raw value never reaches the mart — plus a quarantine report where the gate BLOCKED an unclassified column last week."
"All our dbt tests pass and the metric matches the source count."
"We use SELECT * so we never miss a column, and the warehouse is access-controlled."
privacy-governance.explanation: Only option 2 points to enforced, traceable evidence: a column-level classification, the policy applied, lineage proving the raw value never propagated, AND a real quarantine event showing the gate stops the failure. Option 1 is prose (the leak path). Option 3 proves correctness, not privacy — a metric can be exactly right and still expose raw email. Option 4 is the exact anti-pattern: SELECT * is how unclassified columns leak, and table-level access control does not govern which columns flow downstream.

privacy-governance.intro: Prove the governance layer holds — no vibes:
items: Schema check: every column in the source contract has a sensitivity class and a policy from {allow, mask, tokenize, drop}. Any blank class fails the check.
Gate test: add a fake unclassified column to the source and run the pipeline — it must RAISE and quarantine, not warn and continue. If it continues, the gate is theater.
Lineage map: trace one pii_direct column (email) from source to the served metric and confirm the meta.pii tag survives every hop, and the raw value stops at staging.
Quarantine report: produce the bad-record report naming the exact column the gate blocked — this is the reviewer-facing evidence.
Metric reconciliation: confirm the governed metric still matches the ungoverned count (masking must not change the aggregate) — safety without silently breaking the number.

Explain the difference between mask and tokenize using your own contract — which column got which, and why the metric still works.
Walk the failure path and the repair path on your own diagram: what exactly does the gate do when the source grows a new, unclassified column?

privacy-governance.text: The pattern is invariant across every governance constraint: classify at the boundary, enforce with a gate that can fail the build, and carry the tag through lineage to the served output. Point it at a new data source (a partner feed with a residency requirement) or a late-arriving-data case (a backfill that must re-apply today's policy to yesterday's partitions) — what stays fixed is "no unclassified column reaches a mart"; what changes is the policy set (add a residency or retention class) and the enforcement point. This artifact plugs straight into the data platform capstone: the same data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md carries contracts, DAG/model proof, the quality report, and now the privacy-governance layer — your portfolio claim is not "I understand privacy," it is "here is the column my gate blocked before it leaked."

observability-alerting.proof: The Observability section of data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md: each watched signal named with a concrete threshold, a severity, a route (who/where it pages), and a runbook link — plus one alert wired against a real check (freshness or schema) that actually fires on a bad partition. A reviewer can point to the check that would have caught last quarter's stale-source incident.
observability-alerting.unlock: Every alert in your packet names a signal, a numeric threshold, a severity, a route, and a runbook step — and at least one fires against a genuinely bad partition.
observability-alerting.doNotClaim: Do not claim a pipeline is observable because it 'has logs' or 'has a dashboard'. A dashboard nobody watches at 3 a.m. is not observability. Observability means a specific signal crosses a specific threshold and pages a specific human with a specific next action — or it does not exist.

observability-alerting.text: The exec dashboard read $4.1M in revenue for six days before anyone noticed the source feed had gone stale on day one — the warehouse kept serving yesterday's partition, dbt kept building green, and the metric quietly lied to the board. No test failed, because nobody was watching freshness.

This lesson is the synthesis capstone of the module: it sits on top of source contracts, ingestion, dbt models, quality, lineage, and reconciliation. Observability is the layer that turns all of those into signals that page a human before a stale or malformed partition corrupts a downstream metric.

observability-alerting.prompt: Your dbt run is green, tests pass, and the dashboard renders. Is the pipeline healthy? Answer before reading on.
observability-alerting.reveal: Not necessarily — green means the code ran, not that the data is true. dbt builds happily on a source that stopped updating three days ago: the partition is present, the schema matches, tests on shape pass. The one signal that catches this is freshness — max(loaded_at) vs now — and it is exactly the signal most pipelines never alert on. 'Green build' measures the pipeline; observability measures the data flowing through it.

observability-alerting.subtitle: Source → ingestion → warehouse → dbt → metric. Five detectors tap the data path; each crosses a threshold into the alert router, which pages on-call with a runbook link. The failure path (stale source → green build → corrupted metric) is exactly what the freshness detector cuts.

observability-alerting.title: Wiring the freshness + volume alert in dbt
observability-alerting.subtitle: The real artifact: a source freshness contract plus a custom volume test — the two checks that catch a stale or truncated partition before the metric is built.
observability-alerting.code:
sources:
  - name: orders_raw
    loaded_at_field: loaded_at
    freshness:
      warn_after: {count: 6, period: hour}
      error_after: {count: 12, period: hour}
    tables:
      - name: orders
        columns:
          - name: order_id
            tests: [not_null, unique]
          - name: amount
            tests:
              - dbt_utils.accepted_range:
                  min_value: 0
        tests:
          - dbt_utils.recency:
              datepart: hour
              field: loaded_at
              interval: 12
          - assert_row_count_within_pct:
              baseline: 7d_median
              tolerance_pct: 40  # partition <60% of median = alert

steps.label: Freshness is a contract, not a hope
steps.note: loaded_at_field + freshness turns 'is the source stale?' into a first-class check. This is the single signal the stale-revenue incident needed.

steps.label: Two thresholds, two severities
steps.note: warn_after 6h routes to Slack; error_after 12h pages on-call. Severity separates 'glance at this' from 'wake someone up' — noise-control at the threshold.

steps.label: Schema + range tests on the source
steps.note: not_null / unique / accepted_range catch a malformed partition (nulled IDs, negative amounts) at the source contract, before dbt propagates the corruption downstream.

steps.label: Recency as a hard error
steps.note: dbt_utils.recency fails the build if loaded_at is >12h old — so a stale source stops the metric instead of silently rebuilding it green.

steps.label: Volume against a rolling baseline
steps.note: A partition at <60% of the 7-day median is the classic truncated-feed signal a row-count-only test misses. Alert on the delta, not the absolute count.

observability-alerting.caption: Run `dbt source freshness` on the stale partition: max(loaded_at) is 30h old → error_after: 12h trips → on-call pages with the runbook link. The metric build is blocked, not silently corrupted.

observability-alerting.text: DORA 2024 does not make claims about alerting practice, signal count, runbooks, or alert-to-action time. Rephrase without DORA attribution: 'Best-performing teams alert on fewer, sharper signals tied to a runbook and measure alert-to-action time.' The senior tell is a page you can act on half-asleep: 'orders_raw stale 30h → run backfill_runbook.md §3'. If your alert needs a Slack thread to figure out what it means, it is a symptom, not a signal.

observability-alerting.question: A reviewer asks: 'Prove this pipeline would have caught the stale-source incident, not just handled the happy path.' Which answer is the real evidence?
options: 'We added a Grafana dashboard showing daily row counts and revenue.'

'dbt source freshness has error_after: 12h on orders_raw; running it against the stale partition (loaded_at 30h old) trips the error, blocks the metric build, and pages on-call with backfill_runbook.md — here is the failing run output.'
'All our dbt tests pass and the build is green.'
'We log every ingestion event to the warehouse for later analysis.'
observability-alerting.explanation: Only option 2 points to the exact signal (freshness), the numeric threshold (12h), the failure output on a genuinely bad partition, and the resulting action (page + runbook) — the reviewer challenge from the source pack demands the broken case AND the proof output. A dashboard (1), a green build (3), and passive logs (4) all describe the happy path; none of them fire on the stale partition.

observability-alerting.intro: Prove your observability section is real — no vibes:
items: Every alert names a signal, a numeric threshold, a severity, a route, and a runbook link. If any is 'TBD', it is not wired.
Run the freshness check against a deliberately stale partition (loaded_at older than error_after). It must fail and block, not warn-and-continue.
Point to the schema/range test that quarantines a malformed record, and show the bad-record quarantine report it produces.
Confirm the volume check compares to a rolling baseline (7d median), not an absolute count — a truncated partition can still be non-empty.
Trace lineage from the alerting source to the metric it feeds, so the page names the blast radius. If you can't name what breaks downstream, the alert can't set severity.

prompts: In your own words: why does a green dbt build tell you nothing about whether the source data is fresh — and which single signal closes that gap?

observability-alerting.text: The pattern — signal → threshold → severity → route → runbook — is invariant; what changes is the signal per data shape. A late-arriving-data pipeline watches watermark lag instead of freshness; a streaming source watches consumer-group offset lag and dead-letter rate; a GDPR-governed table adds a lineage-reachability alert so a deletion request can't silently leave a downstream copy. Same skeleton, different detectors, same non-negotiable: every alert ends in a next action. This section completes data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md — the capstone reuses it as the operability evidence, the proof that your pipeline doesn't just run, it tells you the moment it stops telling the truth.

cost-capacity.outcome: Take one real (or realistic) pipeline whose cost or capacity is unbounded, and write the Cost Capacity section of data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md: the per-run budget (bytes scanned, warehouse-seconds, freshness SLA), the guard that trips BEFORE spend or staleness corrupts a downstream metric, and the reconciliation that proves the guarded run still produced correct numbers.
cost-capacity.proof: The Cost Capacity section of data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md: a named budget per run, a pre-flight partition-pruning + freshness guard that can quarantine bad input, and a metric-reconciliation line proving row counts and a control total match source. A reviewer can point to the exact run where the guard tripped and the metric stayed correct.
cost-capacity.unlock: Your packet names a per-run cost/capacity budget, a guard that trips before overspend or staleness reaches the metric, and a reconciliation that proves correctness under the guard.
cost-capacity.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have 'cost capacity under control' because a query is fast on dev data. Fast on 3 days is not bounded on 3 years. Without a partition-pruning budget and a freshness guard, the pipeline is one unpartitioned backfill away from a $9k warehouse bill and a stale metric shipped to the exec dashboard.

cost-capacity.text: The dbt run finished green, the daily-revenue tile updated, and everyone moved on — until finance found the number was 18 hours stale because the upstream orders extract silently stopped at 2 a.m., and a full-table backfill to 'fix' it scanned three years of partitions and burned the month's warehouse budget in one query.

Cost Capacity is the synthesis skill that binds a source contract, a freshness check, and lineage into one enforceable budget per pipeline run. It is Section 5 of the packet you carry through this module: the point where a stale partition or an unpruned scan is caught as a cost/quality failure before it becomes a wrong metric in front of a stakeholder.

cost-capacity.prompt: 'The nightly job runs in 90 seconds and costs pennies, so cost capacity is a non-issue.' Before you agree — what is wrong with using today's runtime as your capacity plan? Answer before reading on.
cost-capacity.reveal: It measures the happy path, not the blast radius. Runtime on one incremental partition tells you nothing about the day a schema drift forces a full refresh, a late-arriving backfill replays 1,000 partitions, or a missing WHERE clause turns an incremental model into a full-table scan. Cost capacity is not 'how much does a normal run cost' — it is 'what is the WORST a single run can cost, and what stops it before it corrupts the metric or the bill.' The invariant: every run has a bounded bytes-scanned budget and a freshness gate, or it has neither.

cost-capacity.title: A cost-capacity budget bounds bytes scanned + freshness per run, and quarantines before the metric
cost-capacity.text: Name a per-run ceiling: max partitions/bytes scanned, max warehouse-seconds, and a freshness SLA on each source. A pre-flight guard prunes to the needed partitions and quarantines stale or malformed input. The invariant: no run reaches the metric without passing the budget and freshness gate.

cost-capacity.title: The cost-capacity guard on the source-to-metric path
cost-capacity.subtitle: Orders extract → freshness + budget gate → dbt model → metric. The gate prunes partitions, checks the source contract's freshness SLA, and routes stale/malformed rows to quarantine. Billing and the auth service are deliberately out of scope.

cost-capacity.title: Writing the Cost Capacity guard, one clause at a time

steps.label: The source contract, as config

steps.label: The bytes-scanned budget

steps.label: The freshness gate
steps.note: Rows older than the 2h SLA are tagged STALE, not silently summed. This is where a dead upstream extract gets caught as a quality failure instead of a wrong metric.

steps.label: The metric, computed on OK rows only

cost-capacity.text: Consistent with SWEBOK V4's Operations, Maintenance, and Economics knowledge areas: a pipeline's cost is an operability property, not an accounting afterthought. The senior tell is a budget expressed as bytes-scanned-per-run and a freshness SLA in the source contract — both machine-checkable in CI — rather than 'we'll watch the Snowflake bill.' A budget a human has to remember to watch is a budget you have already blown.

cost-capacity.question: A reviewer asks for the exact evidence that your pipeline's cost capacity is real and not just understood. Which artifact answers the challenge?

The packet showing the per-run bytes budget, a run where the freshness gate quarantined stale rows, and a reconciliation proving order_count still matched the source contract.
A note saying 'the model is incremental so it should be fine.'
A dashboard tile with a recent-looking revenue number.
cost-capacity.explanation: Only option 2 points to the four things a reviewer can inspect: the named budget, the quarantine event (the failure path exercised), the survived-correctly metric, and the reconciliation. A fast dev run (1) is happy-path theater, 'should be fine' (3) is the guess this lesson exists to kill, and a fresh-looking tile (4) is exactly what a silent stale metric looks like.

cost-capacity.intro: Prove your Cost Capacity section holds — schema check, freshness check, lineage, quarantine, reconciliation:
items: Schema check: the incremental model declares a partition key and an insert_overwrite (or equivalent) strategy, so a rerun physically cannot full-scan the table.
Budget check: name the max bytes/partitions a single run may scan and show the predicate that enforces it — including the worst case (a full refresh or a backfill).
Freshness check: the source contract states an SLA, and the gate quarantines rows past it instead of summing them into the metric.
Lineage: you can trace one order from source extract → landing partition → guarded model → metric tile, and name every hop the value passes through.

Reconciliation: after a guarded run, order_count and a control total (sum revenue) match the source contract's expected figures — and you have one recorded run where the gate fired and the metric still reconciled.

cost-capacity.text: Same pattern, new pressure. A new high-volume source: the budget stays a bounded bytes-per-run, but the lookback window and warehouse size change with volume. Schema drift: a renamed column must fail the contract at the gate, not silently zero out the metric. Late-arriving data: the freshness SLA becomes a max-out-of-order window, and the backfill replays only the affected partitions under the same scan ceiling. Governance constraint: PII in the source means the quarantine path must mask, not just divert. What stays invariant is the rule — every run has a bounded cost and a freshness gate before the metric, or it has neither. ci-cd-data.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have CI/CD for data because tests run in CI. If the checks only assert your code compiles and never inspect the DATA contract (schema, freshness, row-count reconciliation), a stale partition still ships a wrong metric. Testing code is not testing the data flowing through it.

ci-cd-data.text: The revenue dashboard reads $0 for the East region all morning. Nothing errored, every job was green, the deploy went out clean — an upstream feed silently stopped at 2 a.m. and the pipeline happily published the gap as truth. Code CI would never have caught it, because the code was fine. The data was not.

This is the synthesis lesson: it wires the whole course — source contracts, ingestion, dbt models, quality, lineage, reconciliation — into one gate that runs in CI/CD. It is what lets a data product deploy on a schedule without a human eyeballing every metric first.

ci-cd-data.prompt: Your dbt tests all pass in CI and the pipeline deploys. The next morning a key metric is wrong. How did green tests ship a broken number? Answer before reading on.
ci-cd-data.reveal: The tests validated the model, not the freshness or completeness of what fed it. dbt `not_null` and `unique` pass on an empty or stale partition — there are no nulls in rows that never arrived. CI/CD for DATA means the gate also asks: is the source fresh, does its schema match the contract, and does the output reconcile to the source row count? A pipeline that only tests transformation logic ships yesterday's data as today's with a green check.

ci-cd-data.title: CI/CD for data gates on the DATA contract, not just the code
ci-cd-data.text: Before a data product deploys, the pipeline must prove the source honors its contract: schema matches, data is fresh, and the output reconciles to the source. A failing check fails the pipeline closed — bad data never reaches the metric.

ci-cd-data.title: The CI/CD data gate — where a bad source is stopped
ci-cd-data.subtitle: Source lands, the quality gate runs schema + freshness + reconciliation checks, and only a clean run promotes to the warehouse. A stale or malformed partition is quarantined and fails the deploy. The failure path (red) and the repair path (backfill) are both shown.

ci-cd-data.title: The gate that fails the deploy on bad source data
ci-cd-data.subtitle: A CI job that checks freshness and reconciliation, quarantines bad records, and exits non-zero so the pipeline stops before publishing.
ci-cd-data.code:
import sys, duckdb
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

con = duckdb.connect("warehouse.db")
FRESHNESS_SLA_MIN = 90          # source contract: max staleness

# 1. Schema check: contract columns must exist, types must match
expected = {"order_id": "BIGINT", "amount": "DECIMAL", "created_at": "TIMESTAMP"}
actual = dict(con.execute("DESCRIBE staging.orders").fetchall())
schema_ok = all(actual.get(c) == t for c, t in expected.items())

# 2. Freshness check: newest source row vs the SLA
newest = con.execute("SELECT max(created_at) FROM staging.orders").fetchone()[0]
fresh_ok = newest is not None and newest > datetime.now(timezone.utc) - timedelta(minutes=FRESHNESS_SLA_MIN)

# 3. Quarantine malformed rows instead of letting them into the metric
bad = con.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM staging.orders WHERE amount IS NULL OR amount < 0").fetchone()[0]
con.execute("INSERT INTO quarantine.orders SELECT * FROM staging.orders WHERE amount IS NULL OR amount < 0")

# 4. Reconciliation: does the modeled metric match the clean source count?
src = con.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM staging.orders WHERE amount >= 0").fetchone()[0]
metric = con.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM marts.daily_orders").fetchone()[0]
reconciled = src == metric

if not (schema_ok and fresh_ok and bad == 0 and reconciled):
    print(f"GATE FAILED schema={schema_ok} fresh={fresh_ok} quarantined={bad} reconciled={reconciled}")
    sys.exit(1)   # non-zero exit stops the deploy
print("GATE PASSED — promoting to warehouse")

steps.label: The freshness SLA is the source contract
steps.note: 90 minutes is a promise the source made. The gate enforces the promise; it is not a vibe about how old the data 'feels'.

steps.label: Schema check against the contract
steps.note: The expected column-to-type map IS the contract. If the source drops a column or changes a type, schema_ok is False before a single metric is computed.

steps.label: Freshness kills the 2 a.m. silent-stall
steps.note: The mission failure. If the newest row is older than the SLA, fresh_ok is False — the stale feed is caught here, not in the dashboard.

steps.label: Quarantine, do not delete
steps.note: Malformed rows are copied to a quarantine table so you have a bad-record report to inspect and repair — they never silently enter the metric.

steps.label: Reconciliation is the anti-silent-loss check
steps.note: Clean source rows must equal modeled rows. A mismatch means the transformation dropped data — the failure dbt tests cannot see because there are no nulls in rows that vanished.

steps.label: Fail closed with a non-zero exit
steps.note: sys.exit(1) is the whole point: CI treats non-zero as failure and stops the deploy. Fail-open (exit 0 with a warning) is how bad data ships.

ci-cd-data.caption: Run it against a stalled feed: fresh=False → GATE FAILED → exit 1 → the deploy stops before the wrong metric is served. Run it clean: reconciled → promote.

ci-cd-data.caption: The invariant: a data product must never publish a metric from source data that failed its contract. Testing the code is necessary and not sufficient.

ci-cd-data.text: The senior tell (grounded in DORA's four keys): elite teams score high on both throughput (deploy frequency, lead time) AND stability (fast recovery) — hard to sustain if humans hand-verify every metric. (DORA measures these outcomes; it does not frame frequent deploys plus fast recovery as a prescription about hand-verification.) The gate is what buys that: a freshness + reconciliation check that fails closed lets you ship on a schedule, because bad data is stopped by the pipeline, not by someone noticing the dashboard looks wrong at 9 a.m.

ci-cd-data.question: A reviewer asks: 'Show me the exact evidence this is CI/CD for data, not just tests in CI.' Which answer proves it?
options: The dbt test suite passes and the pipeline deploys on every merge.
A CI transcript where a stale source partition trips the freshness check, quarantines bad records, exits non-zero, and blocks the deploy — with the reconciliation and lineage logged in the packet.
The pipeline runs on a schedule with Airflow and all tasks are green.
There is a coverage report showing 90% of the transformation code is tested.
ci-cd-data.explanation: Only option 2 proves the gate acts on the DATA contract and fails closed: a real stale partition produces a real block, with the bad-record quarantine, the reconciliation result, and lineage as inspectable evidence. Green dbt tests (1), a scheduled DAG (3), and code coverage (4) all validate the code or the run — none of them prove a bad SOURCE is stopped before the metric ships.

ci-cd-data.intro: Prove your gate holds — no vibes:
items: Feed the gate a partition older than the freshness SLA. It must exit non-zero and block the deploy — if it warns and continues, it fails open; fix it.
Feed it a partition with a dropped or retyped contract column. The schema check must fail before any metric is computed.
Inject malformed rows (null/negative amounts). Confirm they land in the quarantine table and appear in the bad-record report, not in the metric.
Break the reconciliation on purpose (drop rows in the model). Confirm the source-count vs metric-count mismatch fails the gate.
Open data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md: the lineage map names which source fed which metric, and the packet states what passes, what fails, and what must be repaired before unlock.

ci-cd-data.text: Same gate, new pressures. A new source with no freshness SLA yet? The invariant holds — you cannot publish from an uncontracted source — but you add a contract first and set the SLA from its real cadence. Late-arriving data (events land hours after their timestamp)? Keep schema + reconciliation, but swap a hard freshness cutoff for a watermark + backfill window so on-time-but-late data is not falsely quarantined. Schema drift on a partner feed? The schema check stays; you add a contract-versioning step so an intentional column add is a reviewed change, not a silent break. What stays invariant: gate on the data contract, fail closed, reconcile, quarantine not delete. incident-response.reveal: Almost nothing. ## Incident Response — 2026-07-01 · revenue_daily wrong
- Detection: dbt source freshness on `vendor.orders` — max(loaded_at) 61h > 24h SLA (WARN missed; renamed col passed schema)
- Lineage (source -> metric): vendor.orders -> stg_orders -> fct_orders -> revenue_daily -> exec_dashboard.revenue
- Blast radius: revenue_daily partitions 2026-06-28..30 (3 days); no data loss, values understated ~100%
- Quarantine: 14,204 rows where amount IS NULL routed to vendor.orders__quarantine (renamed `amount`->`gross_amt`)
- Reconcile: revenue_daily(2026-06-29) = $0 -> $148,912 after remap; matches Stripe payouts ledger (source of truth)
- Contract change: add not_null(amount) + column-presence test on `amount`; freshness WARN -> ERROR (block + page)
- Reversal condition: if remap misstates > 0.5% vs Stripe, roll back mart + reindex from raw off-hours

steps.note: Name the exact check that caught it (freshness) AND the one that missed it (schema passed because the column was renamed, not dropped). The gap is the lesson.

steps.label: Lineage trace
steps.note: Walk the graph from the failed source to the corrupted metric, node by node. Without lineage you are guessing at blast radius.

steps.label: Blast radius
steps.note: Which partitions, how bad, and — critically — understated vs lost. Stale-and-recoverable is a different incident than data-loss.

steps.label: Quarantine
steps.note: Isolate the bad rows to a __quarantine table with the root cause (renamed column). Never delete evidence; a re-run would overwrite it.

steps.label: Reconciliation
steps.note: The metric before ($0) and after ($148,912), tied to an independent source of truth (Stripe payouts). This is the proof, not the re-run.

steps.label: Harden + reversal
steps.note: A not_null test plus a column-presence contract and freshness escalated to ERROR — so the next silent rename pages you. Plus the condition that reverses the fix.

incident-response.text: Standards grounding (DORA): stability in DORA is measured by change-fail rate and failed-deployment recovery time, not by raw incident count. (DORA does not use the phrase 'evidence-based recovery,' and its 2024 model separates performance by throughput and stability rather than by 'fewer incidents.') In data, that means the schema check that only tests presence is a trap — a renamed column passes it while the metric goes to zero. Senior responders test the column contract AND freshness AND a value assertion (not_null, non-negative), because malformed rarely means missing; it means subtly wrong.

incident-response.explanation: A green re-run (1) proves 'no exception', not 'data correct' — the same malformed file would pass again. Evidence of a real response is replayable and preventive: the quarantined bad partition (what broke), the reconciliation against Stripe/an independent ledger (proof the number is now right), and the hardened contract test that would have caught it (so it cannot recur silently). A comment (3) and trust in the vendor (4) change nothing about detection.

data-capstone.subtitle: The real artifact: a dbt source contract with a freshness SLA and a not_null/accepted-values quality gate that quarantines instead of silently passing.
data-capstone.code:
# data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md  (excerpt: models/staging/_partner_sales.yml)
version: 2
sources:
  - name: partner_sales
    freshness:                       # freshness SLA — fail if source is stale
      warn_after:  { count: 2, period: hour }
      error_after: { count: 4, period: hour }
    loaded_at_field: _ingested_at
    tables:
      - name: orders
        columns:
          - name: order_id
            tests: [not_null, unique]          # schema check: key integrity
          - name: amount_usd
            tests:
              - not_null                       # malformed row -> quarantine
              - dbt_utils.accepted_range: { min_value: 0 }
          - name: region
            tests:
              - accepted_values: { values: ['NE','SE','MW','W'] }

# Quality gate (models/staging/stg_orders.sql) — route bad rows out, don't drop the run
select *,
  case when amount_usd is null or region not in ('NE','SE','MW','W')
       then true else false end as _quarantined
from {{ source('partner_sales','orders') }}

steps.label: Freshness SLA (the late-partition catch)
steps.note: loaded_at_field + error_after: 4h is the check that would have caught the six-hour-late Northeast partition. Without it, the DAG happily transforms stale data into a wrong metric.

steps.label: Schema check on the key
steps.note: not_null + unique on order_id is the source contract's spine — a duplicated or missing key corrupts every downstream aggregation.

steps.label: Malformed-value contract
steps.note: amount_usd not_null + accepted_range(min 0) rejects the silent null-currency drop and negative-amount corruption before they reach the mart.

steps.label: Accepted-values on region
steps.note: the partition that arrives with region='NORTHEAST' instead of 'NE' fails here — lineage will show this is exactly the column that zeroed the dashboard.

steps.label: Quarantine, don't drop
steps.note: the gold move: flag bad rows into _quarantined so they land in the report instead of vanishing. A dropped row is invisible data loss; a quarantined row is evidence.

data-capstone.caption: Run `dbt source freshness && dbt build`: the stale/malformed partition errors at the source boundary and its rows land in the quarantine report — the metric is never published from bad data.

data-capstone.text: SWEBOK V4's Operations knowledge area and DORA's delivery metrics converge here: a change is only 'delivered' when its quality is verifiable in production. For a data product that means the packet must show the freshness check, the reconciliation, and the quarantine report — not just that the DAG is green. Coverage of the contract is the deliverable; a passing run without those checks is an unverified claim.

The freshness failure shows the gate fired, the quarantine report shows which rows were caught, and the reconciliation proves the published metric matches the source of truth — the exact evidence a data-product reviewer inspects.
